utterances.text: A very good morning to everybody. Madam Registrar, would you be kind enough to please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is can the case number IT-03-68-A, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances, first for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Michelle Jarvis appearing for the Prosecution, together with Ms. Christine Dahl, Ms. Najura Nabti, Ms. Laurel Baig, Ms. Nicole Lewis, Mr. Paul Rogers, and our case manager today, Mr. Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution, to everyone in the courtroom and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and John Jones appearing for Mr. Naser Oric, together with legal assistants, Jasmina Cosic and Adisa Mehic and our intern Dimitri Ternousui.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you so much. In this context, I note that Mr. Oric is not present. Defence counsel has notified the Appeals Chamber in writing that Mr. Oric has taken an informed decision that he does not want to exercise his right to be present at this hearing. For the record, I will read the pertinent part of the letter signed by Ms. Vidovic that was not officially filed but sent to the Registrar on 18 March 2008: "We have carefully considered the matter with our client, and we are hereby writing to inform you that Naser Oric will not be exercising his right to be present at the appeal hearing. This decision not to attend was an informed one and that Mr. Oric understands that he would have been guaranteed the possibility of attending without deprivation of liberty." May I ask Mr. Oric's counsel, does your client still want to waive his fundamental right to be present and at the end of the hearing to have the final word; and if so, can you please confirm this on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that Mr. Oric has been informed of his rights and that he continues to waive his right to be present and to have a final word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the appeals hearing in the case of Prosecutor versus Naser Oric. The events giving rise to this case took place in the municipality of Srebrenica in Bosnia and Herzegovina and its surrounding area between June 1992 and March 1993. At the outset, I will briefly summarize the appeals which are pending before the Appeals Chamber. Both the Prosecution and Mr. Oric lodged appeals against the Trial Chamber judgement rendered on 30 June 2006 by Trial Chamber II. The Trial Chamber found Mr. Oric guilty pursuant to Article 3 and 7, para 3 of the Statute of the Tribunal for failing to discharge his duty as superior to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the occurrence of murder, Count 1; and cruel treatment, Count 2, from 27 December 1992 to 20 March 1993. The Trial Chamber acquitted Mr. Oric of all other charges of the indictment. Mr. Oric was sentenced to two years' imprisonment. Since the imposed sentence was less than the time spent by Mr. Oric in pre-trial detention, the Trial Chamber ordered his immediate release. Mr. Oric filed his initial notice of appeal on 31 July 2006, setting out 16 grounds of appeal. Pursuant to the Appeals Chamber's direction, Mr. Oric filed an amended version of his notice of appeal on 5 October 2006, when he notified the withdrawal of his 12th ground of appeal. In his appeal brief, two additional grounds of appeal were withdrawn, to be precise grounds 9 and 10 -- 16, sorry, 16. The Prosecution filed its response brief on 27 November 2006. Finally, Mr. Oric filed an amended version of his reply brief on 15 December 2006. I will now briefly summarize Mr. Oric's grounds of appeal following the numerical order in his briefs. Mr. Oric's first ground of appeal consists of nine subgrounds of appeal in which Mr. Oric submits that the Trial Chamber made factual findings which were unsupported or unsustainable on the evidence. Within these subgrounds, he also alleges that the Trial Chamber committed three legal errors. In his second ground of appeal, Mr. Oric alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in law and, in fact, in failing to make proper findings in relation to the credibility of certain witnesses' testimonies. Mr. Oric's third ground of appeal deals with alleged errors related to the Trial Chamber's application of the burden of proof. In his fourth ground of appeal, Mr. Oric submits that the Trial Chamber misapplied the standard of proof and makes factual challenges to the Trial Chamber's conclusions with respect to each instance of murder. Under his fifth ground of appeal, Mr. Oric submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law in failing to provide a reasoned opinion with regard to the alleged criminal responsibility of his subordinates, and argues that the various forms of criminal liability the Trial Chamber might have applied to his subordinates are not recognised under international law. In his sixth ground of appeal, Mr. Oric submits that the indictment did not put him on notice of the alleged criminal conduct of his subordinates. Under his seventh ground of appeal, Mr. Oric challenges the Trial Chamber's legal and factual findings regarding both the actus reus and the mens rea of his allegedly culpable subordinates. Mr. Oric's eighth ground of appeal relates to the testimony and credibility of Becir Bogilovic. Mr. Oric's ninth ground of appeal was withdrawn. Under his tenth ground of appeal, Mr. Oric alleged that the Trial Chamber erred in law in its assessment of documentary evidence. In his 11th ground of appeal, Mr. Oric submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law in reaching self-contradictory and irrational conclusion. Mr. Oric's 12th ground of appeal was withdrawn. This brings us to Mr. Oric's 13th ground of appeal that deals with the admission and assessment of the recording of an interview conducted between Mr. Oric and representatives of the Prosecution in Sarajevo in April and May 2001. Under his 14th ground of appeal, Mr. Oric submits that the Trial Chamber erred both in law and, in fact, in finding that he had the duty to prevent murder and cruel treatment by his alleged subordinates. Mr. Oric's 15th ground of appeal relates to the Prosecution's violations of its disclosure obligations and the Trial Chamber responds thereto. Finally, I note that Mr. Oric's 16th ground of appeal was withdrawn. I now turn to the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecution filed its notice of appeal on 31 July 2006, setting out five grounds of appeal. It filed its correct appeal brief on 18 October 2006. Mr. Oric's response brief was filed on 27 November 2006, followed by the Prosecution's reply brief on 4 July 2006. The Prosecution's first ground of appeal is composed of three subgrounds that concerns the extent of Mr. Oric's criminal responsibility for the crimes of murder and cruel treatment. In the first subground, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred both in law and, in fact, in finding that Mr. Oric did not have effective control over the Srebrenica military police between 24 September and 16 October 1992. The second subground deals with Mr. Oric's duty to punish crimes committed before he had effective control. The last subground relates to Mr. Oric's responsibility for failure to punish the crimes committed between 27 December 1992 and 20 March 1993. Under his second ground of appeal, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law in convicting Mr. Oric of the crime of failing to discharge his duty as a superior to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent murder and cruel treatment, instead of finding him guilty of the crimes of murder and cruel treatment that he had failed to prevent. On 7 March 2008, the Prosecution filed a notice of withdrawal of its third ground of appeal pertaining to wanton destruction of Jezestica. The Prosecution's fourth ground of appeal deals with sentencing issues. In its fifth and final ground of appeal, Prosecution alleges two errors of law that have no impact on the verdict of sentence against Mr. Oric but are, in its view, matters of general importance to the case law to the Tribunal. The first alleged error concerns the Trial Chamber's distinction between general and specific obligations to prevent crimes. The second error relates to preemptive destruction of civilian objects. Having explained the reasons of appeal, I recall that in the addendum to the order scheduling appeal hearing issued on 10 March 2008, the Appeals Chamber had invited the parties to address first previously identified questions of particular importance during today's hearing. I will not restate these issues now, but would like to stress that the Appeals Chamber's invitations and the tentative scheduling order are made without prejudice to any matter the parties or the Appeal Chamber may like to raise, and they in no way constitute an expression of opinion on the merits of the appeal. On 25 March 2008, both parties accepted the Appeals Chamber's invitation and filed written submissions in response to some of the questions identified in the addendum to the order scheduling appeal hearing. I would now like, as it is custom, to briefly recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo, and the parties must not merely repeat their respective cases as it was at trial; rather, in accordance with Article 24 of the Statute of this Tribunal, they must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the decision or alleged errors of fact occasioning an miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that both parties have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting the arguments on appeal. Today and tomorrow this hearing will proceed according to the addendum to the order scheduling appeal hearing issued on 10 March 2008. This means that counsel for the Prosecution will present its submissions in response to the questions put to the parties by the Appeals Chamber in relation to Mr. Oric's appeal for one hour followed by counsel for Naser Oric for 30 minutes. After a 20-minutes' pause, counsel for the Prosecution will present its argument in reply for ten minutes. From 11.40 to 12.25, we will hear the Prosecution's submission on its appeal. Following a 20-minutes' pause, counsel for Mr. Oric will have time to respond for 45 minutes, and counsel for the Prosecution will have 15 minutes to reply. There will be a break from 13.45 to 15.15, after which we will reconvene as scheduled. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions, or they may prefer to ask questions following each party's submission. Finally, I would like to draw the attention of both parties to the importance of a distinction between, on the one hand, a Trial Chamber's possible failure to make findings of fact and, on the other hand, to the maybe lack of evidence to make certain findings. Having said this, I would now like to invite counsel for the Prosecution to present submissions in response to the Appeals Chamber's question related to Mr. Oric's appeal. The Appeals Chamber open-mindedly will listen to both party's submissions. It goes without saying that no party needs to make use of all the time allotted to it. Experience shows that sometimes it is in favour of each party to prevent the submissions as short and as precise as possible. The Prosecution has the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. Good morning. Your Honours, the Prosecution's response to the questions raised in the addendum to the Scheduling Order will proceed as follows this morning: First of all, I'll address Your Honours on our response to question 1; Ms. Dahl will follow with argument in respect of question 2; and, finally, Ms. Nabti will follow with our response to question 3, which has not been the subject of a response so far. To turn, then, to question 1 which has posed in the addendum to the Scheduling Order, which concerns the criminal responsibility of Krdzic or other of Oric's subordinates and the evidentiary basis supporting that existing in the trial record. Your Honours, what I intend to do in my submissions this morning is to touch upon three points that arise out of Oric's written submissions of the 25th of March; and, in doing so, I'm going to focus in particular on clarifying the evidentiary basis that we set out in our written submissions of 25 March, in particular that supporting Krdzic's liability. Your Honours, my first point is concerning a matter in paragraph 36 of Oric's 25 March submissions, which reflects a misunderstanding that Krdzic's liability rests on a superior responsibility analysis. We say Krdzic's responsibility is properly characterized as aiding and abetting by omission. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber sourced Krdzic's duty to act, not from the existence of a superior/subordinate relationship between himself and the perpetrators of the crimes, but from the duty that he owed to protect the prisoners in his custody. So Oric's complaints about the Trial Chamber's treatment of Krdzic as a universal superior with no corresponding subordinate vanish upon a proper reading of the judgement. We submit that the Trial Chamber was right to find the elements of aiding and abetting satisfied in respect of Krdzic, and we refer Your Honours to paragraphs 489 to 496 of the trial judgement where the Trial Chamber sets out its findings that satisfy these elements. First of all, in respect of the duty to act, in paragraph 490, the Chamber found that the Srebrenica military police, having prisoners in their care and custody, were bound to ensure their proper treatment; in particular, the commander of that unit, Krdzic, was obliged to select suitable guards, provide a proper space, and ensure that proper treatment of prisoners at all times. In respect of his failure to fact, in paragraph 496, the Chamber found that Krdzic was conspicuously absent from the prisons. This factor, viewed against the backdrop of the ongoing and pervasive mistreatment of the prisoners, confirms that Krdzic failed to act to protect the prisoners in accordance with his duty. As a result of this failure, he made a substantial contribution to the crimes of murder and cruel treatment in the sense of making the commission of those crimes substantially less difficult. Regarding Krdzic's mens rea, in paragraph 496, the Chamber also finds that there is no reason why Krdzic, in his role as commander of the military police, would not have known about the crimes against the prisoners, and that at the very least he must have been wilfully blind. We submit that what the Chamber was saying here is that Krdzic, in failing to act in accordance with his duty to protect the prisoners, was at least aware of the probability that crimes were being committed and that his failure to act would probably assist. Your Honours, this leads me to the second point that I wanted to make in respect of Oric's 25 March submissions, and that is based on the assumption that Krdzic could not be liable as an aider and abettor unless it was shown that he knew of the crimes, and this is reflected in paragraph 24 of those submissions. Your Honours, we say this conflicts with Appeals Chamber case law confirming that, for aiding and abetting, it is sufficient if the accused is aware of the probability that the crimes will be committed; and, in that respect, I point Your Honours to the Ndindabahizi appeal judgement at paragraph 122 and the Blaskic appeal judgement at paragraphs 45 and 50. The triumph's findings in respect to Krdzic's mens rea satisfy this standard. On appeal, Oric bears the burden of showing that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have concluded that Krdzic was at least aware of the probability that crimes would be committed. We say the Trial Chamber's findings, as to Krdzic's mens rea, are supported by two factors. First of all, when he took up command of the Srebrenica military police on 22 November, Krdzic must have known that the prisons had been previously run under Halilovic's command in a climate of prisoner abuse that needed correcting and monitoring. As the Trial Chamber found, at paragraph 496, Krdzic must have known about Halilovic's personal involvement in killing a prisoner. Krdzic had been a member of the SAF staff since 26 May 1992, and he must have known about this incident and the role it played in the removal of Halilovic from the position of command. This is particularly so, given that Krdzic was the one appointed to replace him. The Prosecution accepts that, as Oric has pointed out in his previous submissions, there is no express reference in Exhibit P84, the memo pad, about the mistreatment of prisoners; but there is an express reference, in respect of the 22 November meeting at page 28, about Halilovic's dismissal and resignation and Krdzic's appointment, and it's reasonable to infer that there was discussion amongst the SAF staff about the reasons for this. And, Your Honours, there is other express evidence where the issue of prisoner mistreatment was discussed among members of the SAF staff; in particular, in his interview, Oric stated that he had spoken with both Hamed Salihovic and Ramez Becirovic, who were members of the SAF staff, about Halilovic's involvement in the killing of a prisoner, and they had specifically agreed that this sort of event would have to be prevented in the future. I refer Your Honours to Exhibit 329, tape 18, page 3; and the Chamber makes a finding on this matter at the judgement at paragraph 550. Of course, the issue of Halilovic's involvement in killing the prisoner was referred for investigation and various steps were taken in follow-up. So it was by no means a secret that it had happened. Importantly, Oric also stated in his interview that Krdzic was working together with Salihovic and Becirovic in organizing the prisoner exchange in the October period, and that's Exhibit 329, tape 3, page 5. It's reasonable to infer, given Krdzic's role in the prisoner exchanges in the first period, together with Salihovic and Becirovic, that Krdzic knew about the Halilovic prisoner issue, and more generally that he was aware of the conditions in which the prisoners to be exchanged were kept. Your Honour, the second factor we say is relevant to Krdzic's mens rea is the appalling conditions confronting the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica at the time, which was precipitated by actions of the Bosnian Serbs. The risk of abuse against any Serb prisoner who landed in the hands of the Bosnian Muslims at this time must have been palpable to everyone in Srebrenica, especially Krdzic, the very person who had been put in charge of protecting the prisoners' safety. The Trial Chamber expressly found that the severe malnutrition and psychological effect of being under siege were causing the people of Srebrenica to behave erratically, and was an additional reason for taking measures to reduce the vulnerability of the Serb detainees. That's the judgement at 559 and also footnote 1384. Consequently, Your Honours, Krdzic, when he took up command of the military police, was on notice of an unacceptable risk that the Serb detainees in his custody would be mistreated, and this was sufficient to rise to the probability threshold required for aiding and abetting. But, Your Honours, even assuming that we remove Krdzic from the picture, the Trial Chamber could equally have founded Oric's responsibility on the criminal culpability of the military police more generally. This leads me to the third point from Oric's 25 March submissions, and that is his complaint that the military police cannot be held responsible for the crimes because they are not a natural person, paragraph 46. We say this misstates the point of the relevant legal principle, which is not to impose some form of corporate criminal responsibility; rather, the point is that it's not necessary to identify by name a particular subordinate who is criminally responsible. It's sufficient to establish that subordinates within a particular group over whom the superior exercised effective command, even if they are not individually identified, bear criminal responsibility; and, in that respect, I point you to the sources cited in footnote 20 of our 25 March filing. Your Honours, it's clear that the military police were in control of the prisoners, and they culpably failed to ensure the proper treatment of those prisoners. The evidence establishes that during the second period, when the crimes that we are concerned with occurred, the military police were operating out of the police station building where the prisoners were kept for at least part of the time, and that they were recording and arriving the detention of the Serb detainees, taking them from the police station for interrogation and returning them afterwards. I refer Your Honours to the trial judgement at paragraph 485 in respect of that evidence. They must have been aware of the physical signs of mistreatment of the prisoners, and they failed to carry out their duty to ensure their proper treatment. Your Honours, in our 25 March submission, we have also included an alternative basis on which we say the Trial Chamber could have based Mr. Oric's criminal responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute, and that is in respect directly of the guards who were under his effective control. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber was not satisfied that the guards were identified as members of the military police, but we say it should not have stopped its inquiry there. Regardless of whether these individuals were identified as members of the military police or not, the real question was, by virtue of their function and the role that they played within the chain of command under Oric, were they under his effective control. We say, if the Chamber had asked itself this question, the only answer it could have reached would be: Yes. Oric had a de jure relationship of effective control over the guards. We've given more detailed reasons in our 25 March filing, but in essence, Your Honours, it would be unreasonable to conclude that Oric, at the top of the command hierarchy having responsibility for the prisoners, had put the prisoners in the direct custody of individuals that he could not control. The trial record supports the conclusion that he could control them, as one would suspect, but he chose not to do so. Your Honours, this concludes my submissions on question 1. If you have any questions, I will be happy to deal with them now, or alternatively Ms. Dahl will take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Liu, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, from your statement, could I arrive at the conclusion that -- are you suggesting that the Defence got confused with two modes of the liability; one is the aiding and abetting, the other is command responsibility in relation to the relationship between Krdzic and the real perpetrator in Defence filings on the 25th March? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do suggest that, based on paragraph 36 of Mr. Oric's submissions where he refers to this problem of the Trial Chamber's treatment of Krdzic as a universal superior, that it's implicit in that he is interpreting the judgement as employing superior responsibility as the legal characterization of Mr. Krdzic's responsibility; whereas, we say, if the judgement is read in context in proper light, it's clear that that wasn't the basis for saying that Mr. Krdzic was criminally responsible, but that his responsibility rests on aiding and abetting by omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, you put to us two alternatives on which basis Mr. Oric should stay convicted, so could you please point us to the notice of appeal where exactly you put the other party and the Appeal Chamber on notice that you are challenging the findings or identifying errors of fact or of law committed by the Trial Chamber; in particular, in that what you now call in your alternative pleading, as you said, leaving Krdzic out of the picture for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly this is not a matter that the Prosecution raised in its notice of appeal, and our position is that it was not required to do so. If we had raised it at the time of the appeal stage, it would have been an error without impact on the verdict, because of course the Chamber had reached the same conclusion based on a different process of reasoning. When Mr. Oric appealed the Chamber's findings and challenged the theory of liability applied by the Chamber, as part of our response to Mr. Oric's appeal, we did, indeed, state our position that, even if he was correct in establishing an error on the existing theory of liability, that his conviction would equally have been sustained on the basis that he was responsible directly for the guards. I point Your Honours to the Prosecution's response brief at paragraphs 131 to 132. Your Honours, we submit that a respondent to an appeal must be able to put forward additional bases upon which to sustain the same conclusion already reached by the Chamber in the event that Your Honours were to decide the Trial Chamber's reasoning was, in fact, incorrect. What Your Honours are most concerned with is to assess whether at the end of the day the conviction in this case is safe and is justified. We submit that this is reflected in the approach that the Appeals Chamber has taken in other cases; and, in particular, I would point you to the Blaskic appeal judgement where the Appeals Chamber on review determined that Blaskic's conviction for ordering the use of prisoners as human shields was not safe, but that there was an alternative basis based on his omission to act which would justify that conclusion and the Appeals Chamber sustained it on that basis. But my colleague Ms. Nabti will address you further in respect of those relevant legal precedents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But, nevertheless, because this might be crucial, is it your point that when the Defence raises an appeal and you answer in response, that this amounts to an appeal of your own, or wouldn't it be correct to expect the Prosecution to point itself to an alleged error of the Trial Chamber already in the notice of appeal?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We submit that it is not incumbent upon the Prosecution to raise in the notice of an appeal an error which based on the judgement as it stands had no impact on the verdict. If the Chamber has reached the same conclusion that we would advocate for under the alternative basis, on the basis that they've used in the judgement, then at that stage it is a harmless error. It's only at the point where Your Honours, if Your Honours reach the point of being satisfied that the existing basis is erroneous, it's at that point that the issue arises. We say we have properly raised it in the response brief. The Defence have had notice of this additional basis of liability; and, of course, Your Honours' questions have given a further chance to the parties to explore it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe I will come back to this question at a later point in time. Leaving for a second the role of chairing this Appeals Chamber, as a personal note, I think in the civil law system, this would be without any problem that we have to take together all the submissions of both parties. But here I think we need, maybe later during the hearing, further clarification on this formal approach, whether the response by the Defence can amount finally to an appeal on the part of the Prosecution. But for the time being, thank you so much. Maybe you can dwell on this later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May it please the Court. I will address the second question and endeavor to be brief so as to allow my colleague, Ms. Nabti, sufficient time to address orally question 3 which has not had the benefit of a written submission. In the second question, the Chamber asked what evidence in the trial record supports or rebuts the allegation that Naser Oric knew or had reason to know that the military police detained Serbs and that his subordinates aided and abetted crimes against them. In paragraph 560 of the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Oric knew of the cruel treatment and murder of prisoners between September and October of 1992, and that this actual knowledge gave him reason to know of the four murders and cruel treatment of five others at the police station and the building between December 1992 and March 1993. The Trial Chamber considered that Oric must have seen the injuries visibly apparent when he visited the detainees. They were covered with blood, and some could not stand. These severe injuries could not have happened in a custodial setting without the involvement of the guards and their superiors, either by inflicting the injuries themselves or failing to protect the prisoners against outsiders coming in to treat them cruelly. The Trial Chamber also found that specific information concerning acts of murder and cruel treatment was readily available from Mr. Oric's subordinates, men that Mr. Oric knew were charged with the care and protection of the prisoners, their interrogation and detention while the prisoners awaited exchange. Mr. Oric did not concern himself with these matters, despite his position as commander of the Srebrenica armed forces, his knowledge of the obligation to care for the safety and well being of prisoners of war, and his admitted appreciation of the obvious risk of abuse these prisoners faced at the hands of soldiers and civilians alike. The injuries sustained by the detained Serbs were visible and so severe that Mr. Oric must have noticed them when he saw the prisoners. One need only see the prisoners to know that they were being cruelly mistreated. Here we see Veselin Sarac, the way he looked the day he was exchanged. These are frames from the video admitted into evidence as P98. Fellow detainee Radic testified that this was how Mr. Sarac looked the day he was detained. If I may return to the first picture, so that all the members of the Bench can see it. This was from 16 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Am I correct that it was two minutes and four minutes later?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could move backwards to the first picture, please, I think I read - yes, you can see it - 1524, 1526, 1530. So this was a row of pictures taken at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These are still frames taken from the video. Rather than play the entire video, I thought it appropriate to simply reflect the extent of the injuries that were visibly apparent from Mr. Sarac the day he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But before leaving this picture, where in the judgement can you find any finding or where in the appeal record can you find any evidence that the injuries that led to this picture were -- or that Mr. Sarac received these injuries in the detention unit and not during the combat before he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The victim in this instance, Mr. Sarac, did not testify, but several of the prisoners who were in detention with him did testify; and the Trial Chamber, in making findings about Mr. Sarac, relied on the testimony of Messrs. Radic and Zigic. They indicated that he was beaten in the -- while he was detained and that he looked like this the day he was exchanged. They were also beaten and described what had happened to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also considered that Mr. Oric had the opportunity to see Sarac in this condition. He took him out with him to put him on the radio during negotiations for a prisoner exchange. The transcript of the negotiations is at P97. The negotiations were intercepted and recorded. That is in evidence at P97; the translation is at P97.E. At trial, Mr. Radic, who was detained with Sarac, confirmed that Sarac was, in fact, taken out to participate in the negotiations. This testimony is found at the transcript at page 3567. Radic testified that Oric saw them the night before they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Judge Liu has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. But however could I put you a very simple question and that is: What the superior should have to know. In your case from your presentation up to now, it gives me the impression that the superior should have to know -- should have the reason to know the crime has been committed as distinct from the reason to know the subordinate's criminal conduct is sufficient to hold an accused responsible under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In the context of crimes such as these that occur in a prison setting, they are one and the same. When prisoners who are under guard and kept in locked cells are covered with blood, have had teeth broken and extracted, are bruised, and, indeed, as Mr. Zigic testified had fresh blood, when the person in whose care these prisoners have been entrusted sees this, this information is sufficiently alarming that he should investigate further. Prisoners cannot be cruelly mistreated in a locked environment without the assistance of the person at the door. The visible injuries of these prisoners and the death of some raises the strong inference that either the guards are perpetrating the criminal mistreatment and inflicting the injuries that accuse the death, or that they are assisting others to cruelly mistreat the prisoners by letting them in. The testimony of the prisoners was that they were kept in a locked cell under guard, that there were bars on the windows, that their movements were controlled. One testified that whenever a particular guard showed up -- a soldier showed up, they gave him the key, Beli, and that he was able to take them. The prisoners said that they were beaten when they were allowed into the hallway to go to use the lavatory, and that some testified also that they were beaten during the interrogations as well. This point addresses, of course, question four that was put to the Prosecution. Once a superior knows that his detainees have been assaulted or murdered, by that very fact, he needs to investigate and find out how that happened. The controlled environment should protect the prisoners from outsiders' abuse. This is the same situation confronted by the Krnojelac Trial Chamber, which found that Krnojelac had reason to know of the involvement of the guards in the crimes against the detainees there. The guards were in direct contact with and controlled the detainees. Therefore, the Trial Chamber in Krnojelac considered that some of them must have been involved. That finding was at paragraph 318 of the trial judgement. The Appeals Chamber agreed, finding that knowledge of one act of torture against a prisoner was sufficiently alarming information so as to have alerted Krnojelac to the risk that more acts of torture were being committed or were about to be committed. That finding in the appeals judgement can be found at paragraph 169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So your position is that Mr. Oric had a reason to know that his subordinates aided and abetted by omission the mistreatment of the detainees; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To make the picture complete, is there any finding that Mr. Oric himself saw the situation in the detention camp, in particular when Mr. Halilovic was no longer in office and replaced by Mr. Krdzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber imputed knowledge to Mr. Oric based on the actual information that he knew about during September and October of 1992. The Trial Chamber found, with respect to the cruel treatment and murder between December 1992 and 1993, that Mr. Oric did not avail himself of the readily available information from the persons, his deputies, who he knew were in contact with the detainees. For instance, the Trial Chamber rejected as not credible Mr. Oric's denial of knowledge that there were Serbs being detained at the building. That is at Trial Chamber paragraph 554. He knew that his deputy frequently visited detainees there. Mr. Tursunovic was involved in checking on the detainees' conditions. Many of the prisoners testified that Mr. Tursunovic saw them frequently and inquired as to their well being. Mr. Oric was also present at a meeting in December 1992 where the use of a building as a prison or a detention facility was discussed. The Trial Chamber considered that Mr. Oric simply didn't concern himself with the well being of prisoners because he had, in his view, more important matters to attend to. These findings are at paragraphs 558, 559, and the ultimate conclusion is reached at 560.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. This brings me to the point raised by your colleague, Ms. Jarvis, when she submitted that the conspicuous absence or the wilful blindness of Mr. Oric amounts to the awareness of the probability which is a test in both Ndindabahizi and Blaskic. Is it your both that indeed conspicuous absence and wilful blindness, and you just mentioned that he had to deal, first of all, with other matters, this suffices to fulfil the test as set out in Ndindabahizi and Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I think that Ms. Jarvis's submission pertained to Mr. Krdzic's wilful blindness. But, in this instance, Mr. Oric is liable because he had actual knowledge of sufficiently alarming information that triggers a duty to investigate, to further inquire. When he sees prisoners beaten and bloody, he knows that something is going terribly wrong in their detention. In his interview, he admitted knowing of the risk of retaliation and reprisals faced by prisoners. In discussing the removal of Mr. Halilovic, he acknowledged the difficulty of imprisoning Halilovic for, in his view, killing a Chetnik, because how could he explain to his people what the difference was once that Chetnik became a prisoner. In this, in the area of care and protection of prisoners of war, there is a specific, affirmative obligation to make sure that the prisoners are well-treated. There needs to be a system of monitoring in place. Commanders need to make themselves aware of what is happening to ensure their safety. It is a very dangerous time for prisoners, and international law requires that they be safe. In this instance, these people, the prisoners, faired even worse under Krdzic's tenure than they did under Halilovic. Where Mr. Oric had turned his attention to matters he considered more important in his view than checking on his prisoners, he fails in his duty to investigate the alarming information that the Trial Chamber found he had actual knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: At this point, I would like to turn the proceedings to Ms. Nabti to address the next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NABTI
utterances.text: Your Honours have asked what the appropriate course of action would be if you were to find that the Trial Chamber failed to make the proper factual findings on legal elements required for Oric's conviction under Article 7(3) of the Statute. The Prosecution responds that, according to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, the appropriate course is to determine whether the Trial Chamber's ultimate findings with respect to Oric's criminal conviction are sustained on the trial record. This approach is consistent with the Appeals Chamber's corrective function under Article 25 of the Statute, which includes the discretion to revise the decisions taken by the Trial Chamber where appropriate. It also accords with the Appeals Chamber's ultimate role: To prevent miscarriages of justice. This applies both with respect to safeguarding the rights of the accused and with respect to ensuring that verdicts that are well-supported by the evidence are upheld. An acquittal is not in the interests of justice where the evidence proves the legal elements underline the conviction. In making this assessment, the Appeals Chamber may consider factual evidence in the trial record, in addition to factual findings referred to in the trial judgement. To this end, the parties have directed the Appeals Chamber to the portions of the trial record they deem relevant. The Defence have urged that, if the Appeals Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber convicted Oric without making proper findings, it must reverse his convictions and find him not guilty. This is incorrect because reversal of a conviction is not appropriate where evidence supports the conviction. The evidence may sustain a conviction even where the Appeals Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber failed to make proper findings on that evidence. With respect to the Defence's concern that the Appeals Chamber would be sitting at a second Trial Chamber, in assessing whether the Trial Chamber's findings on Oric's criminal responsibility are sustained on the trial record, the Appeals Chamber still owes deference to the Trial Chamber's factual findings and evaluates the evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. NABTI
utterances.text: -- in that context. This does not preclude the Appeals Chamber from performing its corrective function and revising the decision of the Trial Chamber where it has made improper or inadequate findings; rather, this Chamber has found that the appropriate course of action in such a case is to determine whether the conviction is sustained on the trial record. This is the case both where the Appeals Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber has failed to make clear and complete findings on each legal element required for a conviction and where it finds the Trial Chamber has not properly addressed the elements of the appropriate theory of criminal responsibility or mode of liability. With Your Honours' indulgence, I would like to touch briefly on a few examples. Where the Trial Chamber has failed to make clear and express factual findings on each element of the crime, the Appeals Chamber has found it appropriate to ascertain whether all legals were, indeed, established on the trial record. As you will recall, in Kordic, the appellant had argued that the Trial Chamber had committed errors of law by failing to make explicit findings and give a reasoned explanation with respect to each necessary element of each crime committed. The Appeals Chamber agreed and found, at paragraph 384, that the Trial Chamber did not make specific explicit factual findings with regard to each element of the crimes; although, the Trial Chamber had expressly concluded that the crimes were established. Your Honours, I refer you to paragraph 386 of the appeal judgement which should be coming up on the screen before you, and I quote in relevant part: "The Appeals Chamber considers ... that this does not automatically lead to a dismissal of the charges and ... that, in this particular circumstance, the issue before it is to establish whether the Trial Chamber's findings that the crimes were established are sustained on the record." This Chamber found, that under the circumstances, it was required to re-assess a plethora of evidence in order to find out whether or not all constituent elements of the crimes were established during trial. For example, the Trial Chamber had failed to make specific findings with respect to the elements of the crime of unlawful attack on civilians. There was no finding that civilians were actually killed in a particular attack. At paragraphs 410 through 413, the Appeals Chamber looked to the trial record to assess whether a reasonable trier of fact could have concluded beyond a reasonable doubt that numerous civilians were targeted and killed in the relevant time and location. In its assessment, the Appeals Chamber made factual findings beyond those expressly made in the trial judgement. The Appeals Chamber ultimately, concluded at paragraph 415, that on the basis of this evidence that was before the Trial Chamber, a reasonable trier of fact could come to the conclusion beyond reasonable doubt that the elements of the crime had been met. Another type of case where the Trial Chamber has failed to make proper findings on a particular -- is a case where the Trial Chamber has failed to make proper findings on a particular theory of criminal responsibility or mode of liability. For example, in the Aleksovski appeal, at paragraphs 170 and 171, the Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber did not make necessary findings regarding Aleksovski's individual responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute for mistreatment of prisoners outside the compound. According to the appeals judgement, the Trial Chamber did not make these findings because it misconstrued the Prosecution's theory of the accused's individual responsibility under Article 7(1), in that it evaluated the evidence based on Aleksovski's direct participation in the criminal act, rather than participation by way of aiding and abetting. In evaluating this deficiency, the Appeals Chamber noted that considerable evidence had been provided by the prisoners of their mistreatment when they were digging trenches outside the prison. The Appeals Chamber then recounted and relied upon this testimony in paragraphs 165 through 169. The Trial Chamber had considered the testimony of these witnesses elsewhere in the trial judgement, but it had not made express factual findings with respect to their testimony regarding mistreatment outside the prison. The Trial Chamber had found that the poor physical state of the prisoners who returned from digging trenches had established that Aleksovski was aware of the traumas suffered by the detainees. The Appeals Chamber's conclusion should be appearing on your screen. It found at paragraph 172, I quote: "The Appeals Chamber accepts that the only finding which could reasonably have been made by the Trial Chamber, in light of its other findings, is that the appellant was individually responsible for mistreatment by the HVO soldiers outside the prison by way of having aided and abetted in it. Any finding to the contrary would have been unreasonable in those circumstances. The Appeals Chamber accordingly makes that finding." A further example, in Blaskic, this Court found, at paragraphs 659 to 670 of the appeal judgement, that the Trial Chamber's reasoning in convicting Blaskic under Article 7(1) for ordering the use of civilian detainees as human shields was flawed, yet it did not undermine the conviction. Despite finding that there was a lack of evidence for ordering, the Appeals Chamber affirmed Blaskic's conviction under Article 7(1) as "correct in substance," based on the alternative theory of criminal responsibility through omission. I note that in Blaskic the Prosecution did not appeal the Trial Chamber's failure to initially convict Blaskic on the basis of omission liability. In confirming this conviction, under Article 7(1) the Appeals Chamber relied on the Trial Chamber's findings regarding Blaskic's knowledge that human shields were being used. It then made additional findings on the remaining elements of Article 7(1) through omission, relying on the mode of liability through omission based on the trial record. I refer you again to your screens for the Appeals Chamber's conclusion. At paragraph 670, it stated: "The Appeals Chamber concludes that the appellant's conviction for the use of human shields ... was correct in substance; however, in the absence of proof that he positively ordered the use of human shields, the appellant's criminal responsibility is properly expressed as an omission pursuant to Article 7(1) as charged in the Second Amended Indictment. The Appeals Chamber accordingly finds that the elements constituting the crime of inhuman treatment have been met. There was an omission to care for protected persons which was deliberate and not accidental, caused serious mental harm, and constituted a serious attack on human dignity." Although those particular findings had not been made by the Trial Chamber, Blaskic's conviction under Article 7(1) was affirmed on this alternative basis. Finally, Your Honours will find another such example in the Simic appeal, in which this Chamber rejected the Trial Chamber's finding of criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) pursuant to a theory of JCE, yet then found Simic responsible as an aider and abettor based on the Trial Chamber's findings as supported by other evidence in the trial record. I would point Your Honours to findings at paragraphs 75 through 77, 130 through 138 of the appeal judgement, and footnote 391. In sum, should the Appeals Chamber find that the Trial Chamber failed to make the proper factual findings on the legal elements required for Oric's conviction under Article 7(3) of the Statute, it should then assess whether those elements are otherwise met based on the Trial Chamber's findings and the underlying trial record. Those are my submissions unless you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no questions. Thank you for staying exactly in time because the Prosecution started ten minutes later. Thank you for this, and now we have the time for the Defence to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. May it please Your Honours, in the next hour, I'm going to deal with five main issues. First, I'm going to deal with the inaccuracies in the Prosecution's references to the evidence, both today and in their written submissions; second, I'm going to identify the core fallacies in the judgement which also re-appear in the Prosecution's arguments; and, thirdly, I'm going to discuss the guards as a topic because that's the key issue in many ways, who were the guards, who were they under in terms of hierarchy; fourth, the Prosecution's new theory - and I emphasise that, new theory - of aiding and abetting by omission which was not in the indictment, which was not a trial issue, and which was in any event not proved. And at the outset, I would say in response to the first question by Judge Liu, we're certainly not confused about aiding and abetting by omission or liability under 7(3). We're having to respond to a Trial Chamber judgement which doesn't make the basis of liability clear, and the Prosecution themselves admit that, it's in their response brief, paragraph 126: "The Trial Chamber did not expressly designate the legal classification for the responsibility of the SMP for the crimes of murder and cruel treatment." So the Prosecution, themselves, admit it's not clear in the judgement. The Prosecution are coming up with new theories all the time. It's a different case we hear today from the case which was in the indictment. So we're having to respond to all these different possible arguments, possible bases of liability. We're not confusing anything. It's what we call a belt and braces approach. We're making sure we've covered all the bases. In relation to -- I'm sorry, my fifth topic will be dealing with the Prosecution's argument that the guards were Oric's subordinates even if they weren't members of the MP, and that is in your argument, too. In relation to a question asked by Your Honour Judge Schomburg, and the suggestion by the Prosecution that they can defend the conviction on a different basis from that which is in the judgement, that might be the case, but that alternative basis still has to be in the indictment, it still has to be a trial issue. It's not the case that the Prosecution didn't need to raise it in their appeal, because consider that argument that the guards were subordinated of Oric even if they weren't in the MP. That would be a ground for their ground 1, their appeal, and they didn't put it in their notice of appeal. So they thought of it later, and they should have raised it in their own appeal. That also goes to question 3 and its idea that the Appeals Chamber can make findings and see whether the decision is sustainable. Blaskic, in Blaskic, the indictment contained charges brought under 7(1) and 7(3), so it was in the indictment. We're in a totally different situation here where you're being invited to uphold a conviction on a place which was not ever pleaded. Now, because time is so short, I fear my -- I may run out of time before correcting all the inaccuracies in the submissions, oral and written, of the Prosecution. So I'm just going to give a few examples, and I trust and know that the very competent representatives of the Chamber or assistants, rather, will check the references very carefully page by page, because appearances can be very deceptive. Perhaps there's know more eloquent deception than the video which we saw, because anyone seeing that would think that's terrible that they were in that shape and that Oric saw them in that condition. But it's completely false, and you know it's completely false. If you go back to the trial record, you'll see two things. Firstly, you'll see that Zigic -- sorry, Radic repeatedly said that there were no visible injuries on their faces. This is at P3619 to 3622, and, in fact, the transcript will appear on your pages as we go along, where he was asked -- or he confirmed, rather, that it was dark in the morning and the evenings in the cells. "Q. So in fact it was very hard to see any real detail of people's faces in the cell? "A. It was difficult to see ..." We need to switch to the Defence -- we need to ask the technical booth to switch so we can see the transcript, but I'm going to, given the shortness of time -- Now, there it is. "Q. So in fact it was very hard to see any real detail of people's faces in the cell? "A. It was difficult to see, that's one thing; secondly, there were no visible injuries on our faces." He said it again: "You couldn't discern the details of injuries on our faces." That's at 3629: "Our faces." He wasn't just speaking of himself, and he explained why. This is at 3613: "In terms of beatings, you also told us yesterday that Kemo and the others hit you on the chest mostly to avoid leaving visible marks? "A. Yes, I did state that and that is true. "Q. My question is: Isn't it right, then, that the people who beat you didn't want there to be signs that they were beating you?" The answer is: "Probably." Then in this video, P98, both Zigic and Radic - one of them appeared in that video - testified that the detainees were cleaned up that morning before being exchanged, and that the worst injuries actually occurred on that day. And you'll find that at Zigic, 16/12/04, T3319. "Q. Mr. Radic doesn't seem to have any bruises or injuries on his face; do you agree?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "A. I agree that I do not see any because in the morning we were told wash off everything down to the last drop of blood from ourselves." And so all the injuries you see, all the blood occurred after the last occasion on which they would allegedly have been seen by Oric."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm told to slow down. I'm going as slowly as I can. They testified, Zigic and Radic, that the worst wounds of the detainees occurred on the day of their release, and we'll provide the reference to that in a moment. So, in fact, when you look at the Trial Chamber's judgement, you'll see that they weren't necessarily satisfied that Oric had seen any of these signs of injuries. And if you look at footnote 1500 of the judgement, the Chamber says: "However, even if one were to assume arguendo that the accused did not have actual knowledge of cruel treatment, the conclusion would still be that from the moment he became aware of the killing of Kukic he was on notice." So they've left open the possibility that Oric did not have actual knowledge of mistreatment, and so evidently the Chamber was not necessarily satisfied that he had seen his signs of injury. Some other matters which are in the written submissions and raised today. Paragraph 12 of the Prosecution's written submissions, they say: "Witnesses also confirmed that Oric visited the detainees at the hospital, where they were under armed guard." And they cite Mujkanovic and Ivanovic. But Ivanovic said nothing at all about Oric visiting detainees at the hospital, and you can see that for yourself at T4086 to 4088. And Mujkanovic in fact, denied knowing of any Serb detainees. That's at T5000. So his later answer has to be seen in that light. I mention this illustrations just to show how deceptive their submissions can be of the obvious knowledge on the part of Oric or the others. As far as Krdzic is concerned, Oric in his interview never said Krdzic was physically present at an exchange of prisoners; so for any assumption that he must have known of injuries, that evaporates, too. Nikolic didn't say that Oric "participated in the transportation -- his transportation out of the field to Srebrenica," that's paragraph 14 of the written submissions, rather, they shared part of a journey together to Potocari. Just one more example. P97, which was referred to, allegedly a tape of Oric negotiating about the release of prisoners, according to the Prosecution's own records "has not been authenticated." That's D162 that shows that. And Sarac -- sorry, the voice was not recognised as Oric's by Radic, even though Radic had allegedly spoken to Oric and therefore knew his voice. So we said at trial and we still say that transcript shouldn't even say Naser Oric. And so these details matter -- one last detail Tursunovic, there's no evidence that he reported to Oric about prisoners, and you see that in the judgement at paragraphs 523, 527, and 548. So the idea again suggested today that he had notice through Tursunovic was not found to be a fact by the Chamber. And, in fact, there's the classic catch-22 with Tursunovic that if he did inform Oric, then Oric is going to be held of notice; and if he didn't, that's seen as evidence that Oric didn't take a sufficient interest in the prisoners. I'll come back to that catch-22 later. Now, another preliminary remark is this, I've touched on already, but every time the Prosecution presents it's case, we see a different case being presented. You've seen one in the indictment, a different case in the appeal filings, and really a different case today. And for us nearly two years after the trial to have to respond to new legal theories is simply not right, and it's said that well now that this issue has been raised we can respond to it. But it was not -- this is a trial about evidence, it's not about armchair theorizing: Well, surely this would have been the case and that would have been the case. Those are questions to put to the witnesses. It's a question of hard, cold evidence, and that's not we've not seen today. So start off, I want to set out - it's a very useful German word, leitmotif - with certain light motifs which appear in the judgement and in the Prosecution's arguments. I think it is useful to look at some of this issues conceptually. The first leitmotif is what I call a daisy chain criminal liability. It's the liability where Oric is at best three or four steps removed from the actual perpetrators, and we have a slide to illustrate that; Oric to Krdzic, Krdzic to other military police members, who are responsible for maybe guards, responsible for maybe perpetrators, and with the most attenuated forms of criminal liability in between, not in aiding and abetting, but this aiding and abetting by pure omission. Without wishing to sound flippant, it's like the quaint Edwardian song: I dance with the man, who danced with a girl, who danced with Prince of Wales. It can go on forever, this daisy chain of liability. But it's a fallacy because that amount of remoteness is not a reasonable basis for conviction, and the Celebici Appeals -- sorry, the Trial Chamber was clear on that. They said: "Great care must be taken lest an injustice be committed and holding individuals responsible for the acts of others where the situation of the link of control is absent or too remote." That's paragraphs 377 to 378. So where the link is absent or too remote. We say an injustice, a deep injustice, has been done here with an alleged link and it's absent altogether or at least is at the very remotest. The second leitmotif or fallacy is the universal superior fallacy, and we maintain that that fallacy runs through the judgement and the Prosecution's arguments. It's the fallacy of a superior being liable without any identifiable subordinate under him who committed crimes. Let's be absolutely clear at the outset that we're not saying, we've never said, that it has to be someone identified by name. It would be a misrepresentation of our position to say that we're taking that position. We know full well that's not required. But this must be identified by someone, so at least you even know that he or she exists. You have to know at least two things about a subordinate: One, that he is a subordinate of the accused; and two, that he committed crimes. Without that, you don't have command responsibility. The Prosecution and the Trial Chamber is not in a position to say that of anyone in this case. As I say, not identified by name but just someone you can point to and say, ah, that is the subordinate who Oric is responsible for. They've tried to do it with Krdzic; and for reasons which we've tried to set out and we'll continue to set out, Krdzic is not someone of whom it can be said that he attracted any liability. Let this also be very clear that Krdzic was absolutely not an issue at trial. You'll see we have a list of the references to Krdzic, and most of them are about him being a TO commander in Osmace. It simply wasn't an issue. Witnesses weren't asked about what Krdzic knew or didn't know or what Krdzic did or didn't do. Prisoners or detainees weren't asked did Krdzic visit. They didn't show photographs to detainees to establish whether Krdzic visited or not. There's a complete evidential void, and that's why the Prosecution now has to speculate everyone in Srebrenica knew the risk. That's the sort of argument they have to make, because if everyone knew, well, then Krdzic must have known. So that evidence was not produced and that's why the Chamber clearly held that none of the guards or perpetrators could be even linked directly to Oric, never mind being military police. You have a quote at paragraph 530 that says: "As already stated, the identity of the guards and of the individuals who entered the Srebrenica police station and the building to beat detainees is not such as to relate them directly to the accused, especially since there is no evidence that any of them were members of the Srebrenica military police." That was the whole basis of the case, that the guards were linked to Oric by being members of the military police. So, time and again, the Prosecution tries to say that it doesn't matter that Oric is a universal superior without a corresponding subordinate. Of course, they don't put him in those terms, but that's what they're driving at. So you see it in the written submissions and we heard it this morning. That's at paragraph 7: "Oric was at the top of the command hierarchy having custody of the Serb prisoners." But, in fact, that's nonsense. What command hierarchy over the prisoners? There was no evidence of a command hierarchy over the prisoners. There were attempts to establish hierarchy within the SAFS and with the military police. But this is, again, a new theory. I'll come to it in a moment in distinguishing Krnojelac. Krnojelac, let's recall, is a camp warden or a governor of a prison. It's an institution, a prison; he's the governor; and, therefore, there's a hierarchy over the prison. There's no attempt in this case to say this prison had a governor who answered to this other person and Oric was in that command hierarchy, nothing at all of that. So that leads me to the next fallacy or leitmotif, number 3, and that's the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution trying to hold Oric responsible for a non-natural person, a corporate entity. That's been touched on this morning as well and you'll see that at paragraph 496 of the judgement. It's a very illustrative the way it's even worded: "The only conclusion to draw from this evidence is that the Srebrenica military police through its commanders, i.e., Mirzet Halilovic, and Atif Krdzic respectively, are responsible for the acts and omissions by the guards at the Srebrenica police station and at the building." So the Trial Chamber effectively hold the military police criminally responsible. You see the Trial Chamber's own conclusion, and that's why I said it's such an interesting passage, in the misuse of the plural form, because if the military police is responsible, they should say "is responsible," but they say "are responsible" because they are equivocating between the alleged individual liability of Halilovic and Krdzic and the corporate liability of the military police. So the Chamber isn't even clear in its own mind what it's actually doing. Just as an aside, throughout the trial and in the exhibits, the military police was referred to as the "MP," and that's "VP" in Bosnian. So I would just say that the use by the Prosecution in the latest filings of "SMP" is misleading, and they should stick to what was used at trial. It's misleading because you will see "VP" in the documents. You won't see "SMP" or "SVP." That's just as an aside. Now, you'll find the Prosecution's use of the corporate liability fallacy. In paragraph 57 of their respondent's brief, they refer there to "the SMP's past criminal behaviour," so the criminal behaviour of a corporate body. That runs directly counter to Article 6 and 7(3) of the Statute in which it's clear, reading them together, that subordinates have to be natural persons. Now, leitmotif 4 is what I call the phantom military policemen, the "PMP," because when the Prosecution's arguments about Krdzic fail, they go for this "PMP," as they're bound to do, because they know that Krdzic and what he knew or did was not a trial issue. So, instead, the PMP, let me define it, is someone who you don't know, no witness has ever mentioned or seen or heard. But you are asked to assume five things about him. You're asked to assume that he exists; you're asked to assume that he had a duty to prevent crimes; you're asked to assume that he failed in that duty; you're asked to assume that that failure which you know nothing substantially assisted the principal perpetrators to commit crimes, substantially assisted because as we know from Blagojevic you can have an assistance that is less than substantial assistance, you have to assume that; and you have to assume, when he did all these things as phantom military policemen, that he possessed the necessary mens rea. So that's at least five assumptions that you have to make about someone who no witness testified about, in fact about whom there's evidence that he or she existed. In the words of Wittgenstein: "If that's allowed, then anything is allowed." The Prosecution, of course, again don't call him the phantom military policeman, because that would be a give away. They don't know anything about him. Instead, they say in their written submissions paragraph 5: "The relevant SMP members," as if that solved the problem; but, of course, it doesn't. Who are the relevant SMP members? Who were the irrelevant SMP members? They don't know, you don't know. The relevant SMP member is the phantom military policeman. So how can the Prosecution invite you to uphold a conviction on such an extraordinary basis, making assumptions about hypothetical people about who there was no evidence. It's the peculiarly persuasive power of circular reasoning. Someone must have failed in their duty because prisoners were mistreated; and at the bottom, time and again, that's the argument and the Chamber's argument. It's circular because by definition, whenever a crime occurs, someone has failed to prevent it, because if they had prevented it, it wouldn't have occurred. That's why it's circular. But you don't convict a man or uphold his conviction on the basis of circular reasoning like that, that the Oric or the Krdzic, some unknown MP member must have failed to prevent the crimes because the crimes occurred. I don't know if Your Honour, Judge Shahabuddeen, had a question. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABBUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Jones, I was just enjoying your presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm very much obliged, Your Honour. So we say, that in a criminal trial, you need evidence, not a circular definition of liability. So that's leitmotif 5, circular reasoning. And if applied in this way, it would created strict liability, which is the final leitmotif, the attempt to always try to push 7(3) towards strict liability. The Prosecution understandably likes strict liability because it removes the need to bring that very inconvenient thing: Evidence. So, time and again, you'll see the argument in different forms, whatever happened to the prisoners, however it was caused, the MP or Krdzic or Oric is responsible. That's thinly disguised, strict liability. In fact, one of the best titles of a book I read was: "Thinly Disguised Autobiography," because, in fact, many books are thinly disguised autobiographies. We say the title of this judgement should be: Thinly disguised strict liability. So even if Oric and Krdzic were saints, even if they did all they could to prevent crimes, they would still be liable because the crimes occurred; ergo they didn't prevent the crimes and ergo they're guilty. So those are the six fallacies and I assure you they'll crop up time and again in the judgement and in the Prosecution's arguments. Now I turn to a much more factual issue, a very important one: The guards. What do we know about the guards? Well, we know, first and foremost, that there's no evidence that they were members of the military police, and that's a hundred per cent clear from paragraphs 489 and 530 of the judgement. I've quoted 489, but 530 again is in these terms: "No evidence to prove they were part of the military police." Now, that's no evidence, note, no evidence at all, not the merest scintilla or jot of evidence. This is in a trial where the Prosecution was trying to prove that proposition beyond a reasonable doubt. The key question is this: If the guards were not members of the MP, who were they? This leads to the Prosecution's speculation that, well, they must still have been under the effective control of the MP, and you know their arguments of that proposition. But note, even in paragraph 530, it said that they're not even directly linked to Oric. So just to allude back to what I mentioned earlier, this is a completely different situation from Krnojelac, where the Prosecution never properly pleaded, or pleaded at all the chain of command over a prisoner. You have that submission. But, in fact, in this regard, what's important is that the SUP first detention facility was a civilian police building, and that's what SUPs were up and down the former Yugoslavia. They're now called MUPs, and it stands for Ministry of the Interior. It's a civilian police building. So the normal assumption would be that the police chief is responsible for that and is the same as saying that the guards were civilians. But we don't know who the prison guards are. Oric was not alleged or found to be a prison warden or prison governor, nor was Krdzic alleged or proved to be a prison governor or a prison warden. So the Prosecution can't use the Krnojelac argument to say, well, there are unnamed perpetrators but who nonetheless belong to a unit subordinated to Oric, and that's what Krnojelac in some ways is all about. They simply can't get there because the Trial Chamber excluded that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. So, in fact, with the guards, the Prosecution has one or two avenues to go down; and, in some ways, the issues are reminiscent of Nicaragua. They say either the individual guards were directly subordinated to Oric - this is what they would have to say, but that's impossible because none of the guards are even linked to Oric - or they have to say that the guards were in a unit subordinated to Oric. But it wasn't the MP, it was some other unit, a unit of guards. There was no evidence at trial at all of any unit, brigade, or regiment of guards. There was no commander that guards unit. I mean, guards is a job description. It's not a unit, in the context of our case in any event. Moreover, and again it's very important to emphasise, it was never pleaded in the indictment or at trial that the guards were either individually subordinated to Oric or that there was an identifiable unit of guards under his command. We can't emphasise strongly enough how important it is that these things were not trial issues and witnesses were not asked questions about it. So Your Honours might well ask: How could the Trial Chamber find Oric guilty on these facts? The answer, in short, is that the Trial Chamber basically held that the MP was strictly liable for whatever happened to detainees, and they got there through a complete misreading of the third Geneva Convention. That's set out in our appeals brief at paragraphs 323 to 330. In essence, the fallacy is this: The Geneva Convention, third Geneva Convention, quite sensibly says and states: If you have prisoners of war in your custody, you're responsible for what happens to them. You can't shirk it off by saying, no, it was this unit or this individual. You as the state must ensure that they're taken care of. That makes perfect sense in the context of the Geneva Conventions, and it makes perfect sense even to the extent that it's a form of strict liability because this is inter-state relationship. So there's no harm there in saying, and indeed great benefit, in holding states strictly liable for what happens to detainees. But where it doesn't work in a criminal trial where the same structure, the same argument is used to make the military police responsible for absolutely whatever happened to the detainees. Moreover, it's a complete misreading, because Article 12 of the convention makes clear that the detaining power is the state. It's not a unit or an individual. Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'm obliged. I'm sorry if I ran over.
