utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, before the break, I was dealing with this issue that the evidence to establish that any of the guards individually could be linked to Oric. So then there's a question of whether there's a unit of guards that can be linked to him. The fact is that the evidence at trial established that the only persons identified as having a role in detention and being in any unit were Nurija Jusufovic and Zele, who was the one-armed civilian policeman, and they were both civilian policemen. So we're going to briefly review that evidence because, in our submission, it's the crux of the case in many ways. As I alluded to earlier, first and foremost, one needs to remember that the SUP is a civilian police building, in Bosnian. It's the Sekretarijat Ununtrasnjih Poslova, SUP; and that in turn is the building of the public security service, SJB, of which Becir Bogilovic was the chief. We'll hear a lot more about Bogilovic, I imagine, in the course of today. So there's no dispute about that. That's what SUPs, now renamed MUPs, the Ministry of the Interior, are in Yugoslavia. So, surely, the Trial Chamber should have started from the assumption that since mistreatment was occurring in the SUP, civilian police station, that that came under the auspices, authority, and responsibility of the civilian police and the civilian authorities, right up to the civilian War Presidency, the WP, which in Bosnian is RP, Ratno Predsjednistvo. That was the highest authority in Srebrenica as the Trial Chamber found. So, if we look at that evidence briefly, we need to have the Defence display activated. So, first of all, we see Radic, and you have the reference there: "Q. You were in the civilian SUP, and it was the civilian police who were questioning you? "A. Yes." That's at T3695. Let's look at the next slide. Ivanovic was asked about his detention at the police station. It should be there, yes, if we can move it back. He said: "Once there, there were police officers who were bearing blue uniforms, the kind they used to wear in the former Yugoslavia," and that's civilian blue police uniforms. Then we see Nikolic, and it should be at T2721, where he referred to the fact that it was the -- the guards were civilian policemen. It's the next page, yes. "Q. Now, the guards, they were civilian policemen, weren't they? If they told you that, you were able to see that? "A. Yes, yes." So these are three different detainees at the SUP saying the same thing, that they were detained in the civilian police building by the civilian police. Now, the Trial Chamber discounted their evidence to a certain extent, saying that, well, the Serb detainees were least able to see essentially who they were being detained by; but, in our submission, that's not a correct basis for discounting that evidence, because this is -- this was a conflict in which the detainees were from the area, from the very area around Srebrenica. They knew what different buildings represented. They knew what uniforms civilian police wore. It's not like an international armed conflict where, let's say, if a Filipino fell into the hands of the Japanese during the Second World War and would have no idea who were detaining them. These are people from that very area and they know very well what the civilian police building is and what civilian police uniforms look like. Then we go on to D871, and now we're going to look at the evidence in relation to Nurija Jusufovic and Zele. You see from D871 that's a list of members from the Srebrenica SJB, that's the public security station, that Nurija Jusufovic and Elvir Dzozic, which the evidence established was Zele, were both members of the civilian police, and that wasn't in dispute. So, then, when we look at the evidence of Ivanovic, 24th January, 2005, T4004, this is what happened when he first arrived at the SUP and he refers to Nurija. "A. Nurija was standing in the hallway of the police station, and he asked he, 'Chetnik, do you know Pero Milosevic?' And I said, 'Yes, he is my wife's uncle.'" Then we go down and we see that he refers to him then being taken to his cell, to the right of the entrance to the police station. "Once I was just outside the cell, they opened the door. One of them kicked me in the small of my back, and I banged my head against a radiator." So that's Nurija Jusufovic, and the evidence establishes that that's Nurija Jusufovic basically receiving a Serb detainee, one of the detainees in the indictment, and essentially being there as he's placed in his cell. That should tell you something about who, in fact, was detaining these Serbs. He's one of the very few people identified and he's the chief of the civilian police, Nurija Jusufovic. So, in our submission, there's enough there to raise a reasonable doubt that the guards were subordinated to Oric. So that's at the SUP, the first location. And if we turn to the second location, the building, P475, Prosecution exhibit, and this was a list of detainees kept by the detainees. You'll see there, there was a note: "Not knowing whether Nurija was the SUP commander." So, in our submission, that indicates that the detainees were coming into contact with Nurija Jusufovic at the building, the second location, and were wondering exactly what his role was. The evidence established that he was, indeed, the civilian police chief. And, then, if we look at D987, this is a note from Nurija Jusufovic as the commander of the SJB, and this is to Avdic. Avdic, Hajrudin Avdic, was the president of the War Presidency: "Avdic, I have here imprisoned the Serb citizens from Karno, nine of them. They were brought in during last night and they are now here. Please decide and tell us what to do with these citizens." So that's the civilian police chief with Serb prisoners in his custody asking the president of the War Presidency what he should do with them. In our submission, that's very clear evidence of who was detaining the Serb detainees. But then let's see how the Trial Chamber dealt with that evidence. In footnote 1367 of the judgement, the Chamber said: "There is other written evidence allowing for the inference that at another time the civilian authorities in Srebrenica were involved in detaining Serbs as well." But this doesn't relate to another time. The evidence established that it was August 1992, and that's clear from T14660 and T13303 to 13300, and T13304. We even have a video of that, of the detainees from Karno being questioned by Mustafa Sacirovic. That's T866. In our submission, this is a failure to make proper findings. This is a key exhibit, and the Trial Chamber surely can't be permitted simply to reject it with no or with a faulty explanation and yet the conviction still be sound. So we see Nurija Jusufovic, civilian police chief, involved in the detention of Serbs, both at SUP and at the building, both locations. Then we see his relationship to Bogilovic. We see the next slide, and it's from 18 March 2005, T6247. He admitted that he oversaw the work of Jusufovic. "Q. Did you ever oversee or come and see what the work of Nurija Jusufovic was at the SUP building during the time-period of August, September, or October?" This is 1992, the very period, the first period in the indictment. "A. Yes. From time to time, whenever I was able to do so, when somebody would drive me there; but, on most occasions, Nurija would come and see me." He goes on and discusses this Nurija Jusufovic. So this is the very Jusufovic who received Ivanovic at the SUP, being supervised by Bogilovic, the SJB chief. It's all the more reason to take what Bogilovic said with a very large pinch of salt, because essentially he knew that if Oric wasn't in the dock he would be. This is mistreatment in his police station. Then Zele, the one-armed policeman - that's him in D1011 - he also was identified by witnesses at both locations. We see from that Mitrovic's evidence, 18/01/05, T3809. He recalls Zele as being someone who, in fact, took him out of the SUP to stay in another building. Then we see him again involved in relation to the second building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I received a French translation. I'm sure we all did. Guster, if we go back to that slide, 20/01/06 T15462, here Guster was explaining how a Serb detainee was taken from the building, the second location, and handed over to UNPROFOR. He was asked about who was involved in that, and he refers to this one-armed man. Sorry, if we go back to the first slide. Yes. "Q. Prior to this event, did you know of this person," if we go to the previous one, "this person without an arm, wearing civilian clothes ..." -- please go back to the previous one. Just leave it there. "This person without an arm, wearing civilian clothes, who had come out of that house, came to us and told us that the APC had left for Zvornik and not Tuzla." This is an APC that features in the indictment taking him across the Serb lines. "Q. Prior to this event, did you know this person who had one arm missing? "A. No. "Q. When the APC left, did you get to know anything about this man? "A. Yes. We took quite an interest in him because he was with the UNPROFOR men. We started yelling at him, telling him why we weren't able to be evacuated with the APC since we were wounded as well. The people who were close by addressed by the name of Zele, and told us that Zele was a policeman. "Q. After this happened, were you able to see this one-armed policeman." Then he says how he saw him again, and everyone said that he was a policeman. And as it says, it was Elvir Dzozic. There is no dispute that he was a civilian policeman. He pops up again in relation to Svetlana Trifunovic, who was a Prosecution witness who was also detained. She too refers to: "Some Zele who either didn't have an arm or he was wounded in the right arm." So we have Zele and Nurija Jusufovic intimately involved with putting prisoners in and out of cells at both locations. They're both subordinates of Bogilovic, and we can see in the next chart the hierarchy which was explained by witnesses and by the Prosecution's own exhibit, P84, that Halilovic, as commander of military police, and Jusufovic, chief of civilian police, were both under Bogilovic of the SJB who in turn reported to Avdic. We'll later come to all the evidence that Halilovic and Jusufovic and Bogilovic all brought their reports to Avdic in the War Presidency. If we move onto the next exhibit P45, this is possibly the most important exhibit in this case. If we see and if we look at P45 very carefully, all of the people listed there are the victims in this indictment: Dzakic, murder victim; Sekulic, murder victim; Ilic, murder victim; Nikolic, victim of beating; Ivanovic, victim of beatings; Milovanovic, murder victim; Pejic, victim of beatings; and Popovic, further down, murder victim. So you'll see all those names at paragraph 25 of the indictment. This is a document of the committee for mediation and exchange under the War Presidency, the municipal War Presidency. So, in our submission, could it be any clearer where responsibility lies for the very victims in the indictment. It's not Oric or Krdzic or the military police who are offering the prisoners for exchange, it's the civilian War Presidency. We would ask you to think long and hard about that. This is a Prosecution exhibit and it gives the lie to their whole case. D247 is also an absolutely key exhibit on this issue. Now, this is the War Presidency receiving the report of the prison, and the Trial Chamber didn't consider this document at all. It's not referred to anywhere in the judgement, and we ask rhetorically: Is that the sort of thing covered by the Kvocka presumption that the Trial Chamber did its job properly? It never even mentioned this exhibit. This is the civilian War Presidency receiving the prisoners report for 1993, the prison where Serb detainees were held. It's the work report for 1993. As we know, reports were always sent to superiors. The War Presidency, therefore, obviously considered itself the superior for the prison since it received the work report for the prison. So it in turn would be responsible for the prison where murders and beatings occurred. You can see it was a municipal prison, that's how it's referred to. So the Serbs were detained in the civilian municipal prison and the civilian police station, the SUP. Almost the sole basis of the Chamber finding otherwise, not finding that the Serb were detained by the civilian authorities, was Bogilovic, the very person with the greatest interest to serve in saying that the civilian authorities had no role in detaining Serbs. It all rests, as I'm sure you're aware, on this notion that on the ground floor was the military police, and on the first floor was the civilian police, and that people were detained on the ground floor. You've seen that the evidence, in fact, show that there were detainees, Serb detainees, on the first floor as well. It shows also that detainees were taken up to the first floor for questioning, and you see that with Nikolic, 6/12/04, T2605. He's at the police station and he's taken upstairs for interrogation, to the first floor where, according to Bogilovic, the civilian police were based. Zigic too said the same thing, 15/12/05 T3218: "On another occasion, I went to the first floor," because this was on the ground floor where he was being held. "So this time I went to the first floor where the questioning was conducted by the police." So, in our submission, from the above, when you look at the evidence properly, as the Trial Chamber failed to do, we have the answer who were the guards. They were municipal guards, civilian police, and it was certainly enough to raise a reasonable doubt that the Serbs were guarded by civilian guards rather than military. The Prosecution, in our submission, should be asked to explain or how do they explain Nurija Jusufovic and Zele being so involved at the SUP or at the building, if the civilian police had not role at all in detaining Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I apologise. I come to Krdzic in this regard. Krdzic was never seen at either location, either at the SUP or at the building. Now shouldn't the Trial Chamber have inferred from that that it's because he wasn't involved in detention, it was nothing to do with him. Now, instead, they essentially inferred guilt on that basis by taking it to show neglect of his duties. So, in our submission, that shows how unfair the Chamber's approach was and that everything was seen through this prism of presumed guilt. The civilian municipal guards were obviously not subordinated to Oric, and there was never any suggestion of that and it would be absurd. The civilian police was under the civilian War Presidency, the supreme authority in Srebrenica, as the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 250. So that position is not even inconsistent with the military police arresting Serbs and taking them to the prison and even taking them out for questioning. Now, our position is we deny that that's actually what occurred, and that finding of the Trial Chamber is based not on witness testimony but on suspect exhibits which were confirmed by no one, and with a forged signature in the case of P17. As I say, the -- it's possible to imagine a situation in which one authority is detaining Serbs or anyone and another authority is arresting them and taking them for question. So think, for example, if the FBI arrested an al-Qaeda suspect and he's been held in a federal or a state prison, and the FBI take him out every once in a while for questioning, the guards at the state or federal prison are not subordinated to the FBI. They're doing quite a different role, obviously, in cooperation with them. But, as I say, the position is consistent even with the finding by the Chamber that the military police were involved in arrested and questioning Serbs. Let's also recall in relation to the guards that, as we've pointed out, that the Chamber found no evidence that they were members of the military police. We say the evidence clearly shows they were civilian police, but it's not for us to prove that. It's for the Prosecution, it was for the Prosecution at trial, to prove that beyond a reasonable doubt. Since we're at appeal, and this is an alternative basis for upholding the conviction, that the guards were Oric's subordinates even though they weren't members of the military police, the threshold is even higher. The Prosecution has to persuade you that no reasonable Trial Chamber can fail to consider it proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the guards were Oric's subordinates even if they weren't members of the MP. When you see the evidence reviewed and the absence of evidence on the other side, you'll see that that, in our submission, is completely untenable and there's no evidence that the guards were Krdzic's or Oric's subordinates. I move to the next subject which is aiding and abetting by omission. It's right to say that in their written submissions the Prosecution aren't arguing, it appears, command responsibility on the part of Krdzic. It's all premised on this, if I may say, nebulous concept of aiding and abetting by pure omission; and I emphasise pure omission because it's aiding and abetting where the accused is not even present at the scene. We have the Furundzija example also discussed in Brdjanin where an accused is present and has authority and does nothing, that that can be construed as aiding and abetting by omission. In fact, one wonders if one needs the concept of omission because, in fact, his being there and doing nothing is tacit encouragement. But, on this concept of aiding and abetting by omission, first we would allude again to this issue of remoteness, the daisy chain fallacy, as I refer to it. Oric is now to be held responsible via Article 7(3) for Krdzic, aiding and abetting omission, non-subordinates, guards, who in turn aided and abetted probably by omission other non-subordinates, perpetrators to commit crimes. So it's incredibly attenuated form of liability at best. The second, in our submission, is that there is no doctrine of aiding and abetting by pure omission in international humanitarian law. As I say, it is a different matter if the person is present, and that's clear from Brdjanin where the Appeals Chamber allowed for aiding and abetting by omission if the accused: "Held a position of authority, he was physically present on the scene of the crime, and his non-intervention was seen as tacit approval and encouragement." That's paragraph 273 from the Brdjanin appeals judgement. There's no support for the proposition that, in as a matter of international humanitarian law in 1992, there was liability for aiding and abetting by pure omission, and there's no allegation that Krdzic was ever at the scene of the crimes. In our submission, it would absolutely violate the principle of legality to use it now to uphold Oric's conviction, and we'll come back to the question of legality later today. Moreover, the case was never presented or pleaded on the basis that Krdzic aided and abetted crimes by pure omission. As to whether or not the doctrine of aiding and abetting by pure omission is being which the Tribunal might consider now as a possible basis of liability, in our submission, you should be very suspicious about the notion of aiding and abetting by pure omission, as it would completely cover and go way beyond command responsibility, because with command responsibility, you always have a duty on the part of a superior and an omission to fulfil that duty which assists the commission of the crime. So, in every case of command responsibility, that would ipso facto be a case of aiding and abetting by omission. So at a stroke 7(3) would be redundant, but it would go way beyond command responsibility because there would be no need for the Prosecution to prove that there were any subordinates or effective control. So a form of liability for which there's no precedent, in our submission, which would go way beyond command responsibility and render Article 7(3) completely redundant, as well as violate nullum crimen sine lege, is a form of responsibility of which you should be very suspicious. So even if it had been pleaded, it should be rejected. As far as the mens rea, the proposed mens rea for aiding and abetting by pure omission is concerned, the Prosecution's probabilistic awareness standard conflicts with the established authority that aiding and abetting must be intentional. In fact, what the Prosecution has done is taken the mens rea for aiding and abetting where the person is present and applied that to aiding and abetting by pure omission, because they can't cite a single case of aiding and abetting by pure omission, so they borrowed the mens rea from that very different form of aiding and abetting. What evidence is there anyway that Krdzic had this awareness of a probability? At the very most, based on their speculation about what everyone in Srebrenica would have known, would be maybe a possible awareness of a possibility of crimes occurring. But the Prosecution also forget a factual matter, which is that Krdzic was a commander in Osmace, for some 13 kilometres away at an enclave, a zone, at the time, for much of 1992 and only came to Srebrenica in late 1992 to take up his post. As to whether he must have known that he was being appointed to replace Halilovic because of mistreatment of detainees, that's pure speculation. Sometimes someone can take over someone else's post with no idea of the history behind that. He simply knows he's been appointed to a post. We've pointed out, in our written submissions, the complete dearth of evidence that mistreatment of detainees was ever discussed at meetings. In fact, the Prosecution -- my apologies, the Trial Chamber found that the treatment of detainees was not discussed from the start. If you'll give me a moment, Your Honour, just to confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you please could conclude your submissions within the next one minute. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, rather than embarking on a new topic, I'll conclude there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. It's time for the submissions by the Prosecution in reply for further ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. In the time available, I obviously will not be able to touch upon all of the issues that have been raised; and, in any event, many of them are perhaps more appropriately dealt with by way of the Prosecution's response to the Defence appeal which we have time for later. But what I did want to do in the time available to me now is to make six brief points that address issues relating to the first three questions that Your Honours have raised. Perhaps I can start, first of all, with the -- one of the later points raised by Mr. Jones, and that is whether the concept of aiding and abetting by pure omission is recognised in international criminal law or in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal more generally. Your Honour, we submit that it is and that there is ample authority for that in our own case law, that aiding and abetting may take the form of an omission. We refer you, for example, to the Krnojelac appeal judgement paragraphs 37 and 43; the Ntagerura appeal judgement at paragraph 338; and a number of Trial Chamber judgements, for example, the Krnojelac trial judgement at paragraph 88, the Kunarac trial judgement at paragraph 391. There are a series of cases that have affirmed the concept of aiding and abetting by omission. Perhaps, in particular, what I can do is cite to the recent Mrksic trial judgement at paragraph 553, where the Chamber specifically noted that: "Responsibility for having aided and abetted a crime by omission may arise regardless of whether the accused's presence at the scene of the crime provided encouragement to the perpetrators when the accused was under a duty to prevent the crime but failed to act." So we submit that's a very clear recognition in our own case law of the price form of liability that we are concerned with here. Your Honours, the second point I want to deal with is the issue of whether the -- Oric's responsibility, based directly on a superior/subordinate relationship with the guards, was an issue that was raised at Trial Chamber and of which the Defence had notice. Your Honours, I submit that, in fact, one of the clearest indications of the fact that the Defence was very much on notice of this issue are the submissions that Mr. Jones has just given now. The issue of whether the guards were, in fact, under the control of civilian authorities as opposed to military authorities, including Oric, was a hotly contested issue at trial, and it underscores that the Defence was very much on notice that their -- that Mr. Oric's liability was encompassing the prospect that he had a superior/supported relationship with the guards. Your Honours, we say that, if you look at the indictment, it's very clear that what the Prosecution is doing now is not proposing a third new theory of liability, but in fact pointing Your Honours to a theory that was encompassed within the indictment and the pre-trial documents. It was argued throughout the trial, and it would have been a valid basis for conviction. In particular, if Your Honours refer to paragraphs 22, 23, and 26 of the indictment, in these places, it was alleged that the Srebrenica military police detained Serb prisoners, that they were subjected to mistreatment by the guards and/or by others with the support of the guards, and that Oric knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were carrying out the mistreatment and he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish. Your Honours, certainly it was the Prosecution's case at the outset of the trial that the guards were members of the military police. But at the 98 bis stage, in the decision rendered by the Chamber, the Chamber specifically found that the identity of the guards had not been established, and I point Your Honours to the transcript of the 98 bis decision at page 8999 and also 9004 to 9005. Nevertheless, the Chamber specifically found the accused had a case to answer, regardless of the identity of the guards, based on the existence of a superior relationship between Oric and the guards. So from that point, Oric certainly was on notice that regardless of their individual identification, he was defending against a case based on Oric's control over the guards and, in fact, the trial record discloses that he did defend against that charge. In particular in our response brief at paragraph 209, we have pointed out the evidence elicited in cross-examination by the Defence that confirms that they were fully aware that this was a potential basis for their liability. Your Honour, in respect of the pleading issue concerning Krdzic as an individual, perhaps I can just make a general response and indicate that Ms. Baig is available for further questions on that issue tomorrow; but certainly, Your Honour, the pleadings in this case put the Defence on notice that Oric was alleged to have been the superior of the military police who were in charge of the prisoners, and it must be implicit within the boundaries of that that the commander of that very unit, Krdzic, was amongst that group. Your Honours, Mr. Jones has raised a point that I would like to clarify, although it's a small point, and that was his complaint about the Prosecution's use of the abbreviation "SMP" or Srebrenica military police in this case. Of course, this was simply a shorthand way of referring to the military police in Srebrenica, and I think that's clear from the context in which we've used that in the brief and it is not accurate to say that this could give rise to any misunderstanding. Your Honours, to conclude, in terms of the Trial Chamber's approach to the guards and their direct relationship with Oric, we say the Trial Chamber became preoccupied with the label of whether they were military police or not and lost sight of the more significant question whether by virtue of their function they played a role in Oric's command hierarchy. Your Honours, I'd like to underscore the reasonableness of the conclusion we seek to arrive at by pointing out that, of course, the prisoners in this case were militarily valuable assets. They were detained for two main reasons: They were interrogated for Serb military information and they were exchanged for Bosnian Muslim corpses. And we see from the trial record that Bosnian Muslim military personnel were involved with the prisoners from the moment of their capture through to their exchange and the prisoners were confined and monitored throughout, as you would expect. In particular, the prisoners were captured by Bosnian Muslim forces, often during combat operations in areas around Srebrenica. Oric was involved personally in the transport of one of the prisoners, Ratko Nikolic, in January 1993 when he was transported back into Srebrenica. During the course of their imprisonment, the prisoners were interrogated by Bosnian Muslim military personnel. Hamed Salihovic played a key role in overseeing the interrogations, and he was the SAF chief of security and intelligence. The military police were recording the arrival and detention of the prisoners, and they took them from the police station for interrogation and returned them afterwards. Members of the SAF visited the prisoners during their interrogation -- during their detention. Zulfo Tursunovic, in particular, frequently visited the Serb prisoners. And, finally, members of the SAF negotiated the exchange of the prisoners and the evidence demonstrates their continued involvement throughout. Your Honours, obviously these were militarily valuable assets, they were kept in a confined, controlled environment, and it would be entirely unreasonable to conclude that the guards in charge of these prisoners were not under the effective control of the military commanders and authorities, the top of whom was Oric. And we submit that that is a reasonable finding and would support the conviction as an alternative basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes the submissions on the questions raised by the Chamber, and we will continue immediately for the next 45 minutes with the Prosecution's appeal as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll be dealing with ground 1 and subground 1 on behalf of the Prosecution, dealing particularly with the considerations relating to effective control in the first period. Your Honour, the Chamber's error, we allege, in this case was in failing to find that Oric had effective control over the military police in the first period when crimes were being committed. And it fell into that error, we would say, by losing sight of the evidence as to how the military police functioned as a military unit throughout when considering how the armed forces staff, and Oric in particular, exercised effective control over it. And, Your Honours, we're grateful to Mr. Jones for pointing out the use of "SMP" and "MP" because it's right to focus back on this as a military unit, as a military police unit, and not to try to accord it some form of special status because it was in Srebrenica. The Trial Chamber found that the Srebrenica TO, later renamed as the Srebrenica armed forces staff, established the military police, paragraphs 181 and 499 of the judgement. And if Your Honours have in front of you P109, which I hope is displayed on the screen, there is a part of that decision which has been highlighted where you will see in the centre, this is a decision of the TO Defence staff, I hope it's sufficiently clear, dated the 2nd of July, 1992, that: "A decision was made to form war-time military police," and that Mirzet Halilovic was appointed as the commander of that unit. And the Trial Chamber found that the TO did, in fact, appoint Halilovic as the commander. Oric was the commander of the armed forces staff from the 20th of May, 1992, trial judgement paragraphs 141 to 144, and he remained in that position as commander throughout the period of the indictment. And they further found that he was de jure commander of all the Bosnian Muslim armed groups operating in the Srebrenica area during the time-frame of the indictment, trial judgement paragraph 698 to 696. Your Honours, in those circumstances, with the totality of evidence in mind, the Prosecution say that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have then found that Oric did not have effective control. Your Honours, the SMP, military police, was regarded as and functioned as a military police unit from its foundations, and it would make no sense, we say, for the unit to then be somehow hived off or subordinated to a civilian entity whilst the unit was carrying out military functions. In particular, Your Honours, we would show P4, which I think hopefully will be there, yes, P4, showing the foundation of the -- early foundations of this unit. And Your Honours will see at item 10, which has been highlighted, this is before any War Presidency was established, this was in the very early days, you can see at item 10 that: "Services that are to be attached to the Srebrenica TO, one of which is VP, the organization of which to be carried out by Mirzet Halilovic." And, on VP, we're grateful to Mr. Jones clarifying in his earlier submissions that "VP" does in fact refer to Vojna policija, military police. He will remember very well that he made a point act this in his own submissions relating to that, saying the translation was unclear; plainly, it isn't. That original foundation is developed through the other available documents and upon which the Trial Chamber relied. P84, the memo pad of the 15th of October, 1992, pages 10 and 11, show this developing position and the fact that the military police remain within the armed forces structures; and also at P80, pages which we have again here, pages 3, 7, and 8. Your Honours, I've just picked up page 3 here which is a document from -- admittedly from 1993, but it looks back at the formations as they existed. And you can see, Your Honours, that it's consistent with the contemporaneous documents that existed at the time, in particular P4 and the others, where the armed forces come under the operational control -- sorry, the military police come under the operational control of the armed forces. In addition, Hogic gave evidence at trial transcript 8120 of what the functions of an MP unit are. He said that they organized and secured the rear of combat units. They brought in military persons that commit crimes, that they themselves would not go into combat but secure transport, and that they secured prisoners of war in detention and took them to be exchanged. And he clarified that often they would take to the exchange. He said it didn't necessarily mean that they were involved directly in the negotiations, although in this case we say Naser Oric was. So far as the function of the military police is concerned, they may not themselves arrange the exchanges. So when my learned friend relies on the document showing the civilian commission involved with the prisoners, that's not something on Hogic's evidence that you would be surprised to see, particularly as the civilian organizations had developed at that stage. Your Honours, this wasn't a small unit. P590E, which I hope will come on the screen again, yes, is a list of members. This is the second page of that list, it's dated the 31st of July, 1992, and it has the name of Halilovic as the commander at the bottom. I accept that there were challenges as there were to almost every document in this case by the Defence and that some witnesses suggested that some of the names on this list may not have been members of the military police; however, that evidence related to only four or five particular names out of a list of 60-odd. And Your Honours will see the name of Sead Ademovic, forgive me if I mispronounce that to the B/C/S speakers. But Ademovic is listed there, and he produces a report which says document P609E of the 14th of August, 1992, within the normal command structure; and the significance of this document, Your Honours, is that it shows military functions being carried out by the military police. There are a whole series of actions that you would expect them to be doing consistent with the evidence of Hogic. Your Honours have it, I'm not going to go through it, but it's clear from there, escorting the army, that type of duty, rear guard duties are evident. In addition, P84, the memo pad of the 3rd of October, 1992, page 9, paragraph 9, shows that the military police were being used in military operations at the rear. Military police "must take mobile radio transmitters and walkie-talkies." P84, 23rd of October, 1992, admittedly just outside of the time-frame that we're first concerned with here; however, consistent involvement with the military police is being demonstrated here in operational activities and in their military police activities. The SAFO staff decided - it's not the War Presidency - decided that the military police would go to Poluznik [phoen], apologies if I've mispronounced it, ringing to custody guards who had refused to perform duties. This is well before the organizational changes of the 22nd of November, 1992. Your Honours, prisoners of war were being detained within the police station at this time throughout, to Oric's certain knowledge, as is demonstrated by his own interviews. He confirmed what the role of the military police was. P329, tape 3, page 1, he says this concerning the detention of prisoners, he says: "So when they got down there," that is, the prison, "they were handed over to the military police and the military police had its own part of a job to do." No suggestion of hand-over to the civilian police despite the suggestions by the Defence that that was the true position. Why would Oric be saying in his interview they were handed over to the military police if, in fact, it was the civilian police to his certain knowledge. And he must have known because he was both on the War Presidency and part of the armed forces staff. He goes on to say: "Together with -- in coordination with Mr. Halilovic, then Hamed Salihovic," who you know, Your Honours, was the head of intelligence because before the war he had been a military officer, and they go on to talk about further involvement with the prisoners. And he also says tape 3, P329, page 4, that Halilovic was the commander of the military police; he was the prison warden. Your Honours will remember Mr. Jones using that phrase about Krdzic when he made his submission, saying there was no suggestion that he was a prison warden. There's very clear evidence that Halilovic was. And, further, on tape 3 and page 9 and tape 16, page 11, he said it was up to the military police to carry out this part, i.e., detention, this part of the job. There was consistent military involvement with the prisoners from arrest to detention and processing. Salihovic and Becirovic, both of whom were involved with the armed forces staff, were appointed in September of 1992, P79E and P255E. Both of those individuals were involved from the outset, showing military involvement. That is the purpose for referring to them, to show the continued military involvement with the detention of prisoners and a consistent pattern developing throughout the time-period. Oric refers to those as persons to whom Halilovic would report, P329, tape 3; Salihovic was interrogating the prisoners as head of department, P329, tape, page 8. I've said Oric visited the prisons; we've dealt with that, and Oric was involved directly in their exchange, P339, P100E. On the 10th of June, 1992, well before this period of detention, he's involved in the exchange of prisoners. P77E and 78 shows him directly negotiating or being involved with negotiations with Serb commanders relating to release of prisoners. And, finally, of course, P97, the intercept relating to the exchange of Radic and Sarac. Your Honours, as commander of all the Bosnian Muslim armed groups, he has exercised effective control over the military police. The Trial Chamber looked ultimately for hallmarks of effective control at paragraph 312 of their judgement. In our submission, they simply failed to attach appropriate weight and significance to the multiplicity of evidence that showed his control. Among the factors that they are identified with the procedures of appointment for a superior, I've taken you to that evidence already. The power to issue orders, I've taken you to some of that evidence, and by virtue of his position as commander he plainly able so to do. They identified the ability to take disciplinary action. Halilovic was dismissed ultimately by the armed forces staff, P84, page 28; but what is significant is that it was Oric that initiated the investigation into Halilovic, plainly showing he was able so to do and ultimately was involved in his dismissal. That's in his interview, tape 3, page 2. All these references are at P329. He had the capacity to transmit reports to competent authorities, another factor that they identified, in fact whilst communications were functions he was doing that, P266E of the 23rd of June, 1992; and he refers again to it in his interview, and plainly he had the capacity to sign orders. P109, the very order which sets up, we say, this appointment is one signed by him or at least has his name upon it. Also significant, we say, as a small piece of evidence but perhaps important, is P5E admittedly slightly later of the 29th of October, 1992, is an order to MPs from him; and on the 31st of October, 1992, an order assigning a number of the military police as being attached to the armed forces staff, P167E. I'll deal with this a little bit more tomorrow. But when you look at it, you can see that the same code is given for the Srebrenica armed forces staff as is given for a series of other smaller units, and the military police is one of them and takes the armed forces staff code as item 6. That's also consistent with the other documents relating to organization in P80 and P84. Finally, they attach significance or suggested that it would be significant if an individual had a high profile, in other words, what was the nature of their profile. I've already touched the documents P339E of the 10th of June, 77 and 78 of the 10th of July and the intercept, which all show Oric's involvement in the negotiation of prisoners exchanges at that stage. He had that high profile and was commander. Your Honours, contrary to the Trial Chamber's findings, the only reasonable conclusion was that Oric effectively controlled this military unit insofar as it carried out military functions. To hold otherwise would be to hold that a military unit performing military functions was not answerable to the military but to the War Presidency, as is suggested, on all the evidence a fledgling civilian authority struggling to establish itself and establish credibility. It would be absurd, in our submission, to suggest that a military commander would divest himself of control of the military unit of the size of this unit as is evidenced within the trial record. In those circumstances, we would invite the Appeals Chamber to overturn the findings insofar as they relate to effective control in the first period. Unless I can assist Your Honours, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to continue submissions on the Prosecution's appeal by addressing Your Honours in respect of ground 2 concerning Oric's conviction for a separate dereliction of duty crime and also ground 4 regarding the manifestly inadequate sentence of two years that he received. Ms. Baig will complete our submissions and address you on ground 1, subground 4 concerning Oric's responsibility for failing to punish crimes in the September and October period, the issue of successor commander as we will refer to it. Your Honours, we won't in the time available make submissions on other matters in the Prosecution's appeal, but certainly we are available to assist you if you have particular questions on those other matters. So, Your Honours, the two issues that I'm going to be dealing with this morning are both issues that reflect one of the Prosecution's core concerns in bringing this appeal, and that is that the outcome of the trial judgement in this case has the effect of trivializing superior responsibility to such an extent that it no longer forms a meaningful part of international criminal law. Moving to the first issue, and that is characterization of Article 7(3) as we submit a mode of liability for holding superiors responsible for the same crimes as their subordinates. Oric was convicted for the crime of failing to discharge his duty to prevent the occurrence of murder and cruel treatment. He should have been convicted for the murder and cruel treatment he failed to prevent. The conceptualization of Article 7(3) as a separate crime of dereliction of duty is a departure from the overwhelming majority of cases prosecuted before this Tribunal. As set out in the Prosecution's appeal brief, the Appeals Chamber's approach in previous cases confirms that Article 7(3) is a mode of liability for the subordinates' underlying crimes. This is also consistent with customary law underpinning the doctrine and the conceptualization of it in Article 7(3) of our Statute. To the sources we've already set out in our appeal brief, I would add the Kamuhanda appeal judgement at paragraph 75, which refers to superior responsibility under Article 6(3) of the ICTR Statute, as quoted: "A distinct mode of responsibility from individual responsibility for ordering a crime under Article 6(1) of the Statute." I won't repeat the material in our brief, but what I would like to do is focus on explaining to Your Honours why convicting superiors for the underlying subordinate's crime does not represent an unacceptable departure from the culpability principle. The Tadic Appeals Chamber described this principle at paragraph 186 as the notion that nobody may be held criminally responsible for acts or transactions in which he has not personally engaged or in some other way participated. Let me start with failure to prevent part of the doctrine which is the basis upon which Oric's conviction rests. Treating failure to prevent as a mode of liability does not depart from the culpability principle. Although the Blaskic Appeals Chamber at paragraph 77 confirmed that causation is not an element of Article 7(3) that requires proof in all cases, there is inherently an element of causation in failure to prevent cases. This was recognised by the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber at paragraph 193, which emphasised the fact that a superior's failure to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent crimes creates or heightens a real and reasonably foreseeable risk that crimes will be committed. In failure to punish cases, there is no direct causal link between the commission of the crime and the superior's subsequent failure to punish. However, the Tribunal's case law has recognised failure to punish as an acceptable departure from the causation requirement. In particular, in the Blaskic appeal, the Defence challenged the validity of the failure to punish aspect of superior responsibility precisely because there is no causal nexus to the crimes. Blaskic argued that the creation of criminal responsibility for failing to punish a subordinate's unlawful act without any nexus to the prevention of the commission of future crimes must be considered to exceed the scope of the Statute. The Blaskic Appeals Chamber specifically cited this argument at paragraph 78 of the judgement before rejecting the corresponding Defence ground of appeal. The Appeals Chamber went on to uphold Blaskic's conviction for grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions based on his failure to punish, and that's at paragraph 633 of the Blaskic appeal judgement. So the Appeals Chamber very clearly employed failure to punish as a mode of liability notwithstanding the absence of the direct causal link. In considering the validity of this result, we need to look at the issue, not through the lens of domestic criminal law, but through the distinctive lens of IHL and armed conflict out of which the command responsibility concept grew. As the Appeals Chamber emphasised in the Hadzihasanovic command responsibility appeal decision at paragraph 14, command responsibility is derived from the notion of responsible command, which is the trigger for both the rights and duties conferred by IHL. So when a soldier in the field kills another human being in combat, he benefits from the immunity IHL grants against personal criminal culpability because he is acting under a responsible command. Conversely, a commander is responsible for the crimes of his subordinates unless and until he dissociates himself by taking necessary and reasonable steps. That's not to say, Your Honours, that the principle of personal culpability is irrelevant to an assessment of superior responsibility. But the contours of the doctrine as it's developed under international law have sufficient limitations built in. It is not strict liability or even liability based on a negligence standard, it is not liability that can be imposed unless a superior is actually in a position to effectively control his subordinates, and a commander is not expected to be the impossible. His responsibilities are assessed by what is reasonable in the circumstances in which he is operating. In sum, the failure to punish aspect of superior responsibility is a valid exception to the causation requirement that operates within fair and reasonable limits. It's justified having regard to the distinctive factors of the doctrine that find no parallel in domestic criminal law; and, in particular, the special relationship of effective control between the superior and the subordinate and the critical role that commanders play in the enforcement of IHL. As the ICRC commentary to Article 86 of Protocol I notes: "In fact, the role of commanders is decisive. Everything depends on commanders and without their conscientious supervision, general legal requirements are unlikely to be effective."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: The implementation of international humanitarian law, and thereby the protection of the most vulnerable people on earth, depends on the preservation of superior responsibility as a genuine deterrent. That's why a superior responsibility has developed under customary law as a mode of liability for subordinates' underlying crimes, and I submit that's also why the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has upheld this application of the doctrine in cases before this Tribunal. Your Honours, I'll move now to my second issue, and that is the manifestly inadequate sentencing. The two-year sentence imposed on Oric does not meet the Tribunal's main sentencing objectives of retribution and deterrence. A two-year sentence for a commander who chose not to take steps to prevent the murder of four prisoners in his custody and the prolonged cruel treatment of five others does not duly express the international community's outrage over these crimes, nor does it provide a meaningful incentive for commanders in the future to take their IHL obligation seriously and to use their powers to impose order in the chaos of conflict. I'm going to focus in my submissions on just two factors, two of the primary factors leading to the Trial Chamber's trivialization of the crime committed and the inadequate sentence imposed. First of all, the characterization of superior responsibility as in the Chamber's word a mere dereliction of duty; and, secondly, the Trial Chamber's erroneous consideration of the prevailing humanitarian crisis in Srebrenica as the pivotal factor in determining sentence. Your Honours, moving to the first of those topics, as I explained, the Appeals Chamber has previously treated superior responsibility as a mode and not a separate crime of dereliction of duty. In this case, the Chamber was wrong to find, in paragraph 724, that sui generis nature of superior responsibility allowed for even greater flexibility in determining sentence; and in echo of that theme, I would also point Your Honours to the judgement pronouncement, transcript page 16657. The Chamber referred at various junctures throughout the judgement to superior responsibility as a mere dereliction of duty. For example, in paragraph 293, the Chamber said that: "Superior responsibility is characterized by the mere omission of preventing or punishing crimes committed by subordinate others, and further that the superior is held responsible merely for his neglect of duty with regard to the crimes committed by others." The Chamber's approach is entirely at odds with the Appeals Chamber's pronouncement in the Celebici case that responsibility of a superior is not per se less serious than the conduct of the subordinate perpetrators, and that's at paragraph 735. To that, I would also add the 11 bis decision in the Delic case of 9 July 2007 at page 9, noting that the accused is no less culpable for his failure to act under Article 7(3) than he would be for the commission of crimes under Article 7(1). And, thirdly, Your Honours, we have to bear in mind the privileged position of power and control occupied by the superior and the crucial duty he is entrusted with to enforce IHL. The breach of a commander's duty is inherently very grave. Ultimately, the two-year sentence imposed on Oric is solid proof that the Chamber viewed a superior's breach of duty as a trivial matter. Even if Your Honours were to agree with the Trial Chamber that superior responsibility is a separate dereliction of duty crime, we ask you to make it clear that it is not a trivial offence and that it will attract a meaningful penalty. Your Honour, the second factor I'm going to consider is the prevailing circumstances in Srebrenica as the pivotal factor in determining sentence. The Trial Chamber expressly stated that this was its pivotal consideration in establishing Oric's sentence at paragraph 767. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber accepts that the Trial Chamber was entitled to take into account Oric's youth and the enormous burden placed on his shoulders at the time of the crimes, but he was given separate credit for those factors, and I refer Your Honours to the trial judgement at paragraph 755 to 757. Our concern is that Oric should not have been given separate credit for the generally difficult or chaotic circumstances confronting Srebrenica. Your Honours, there is a disconnect between the Trial Chamber's sentencing analysis and the findings in the body of the judgement, which confirm that the prevailing circumstances had no impact on Oric's ability to exercise effective control or to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent crimes. It was his choice to do nothing. In particular, at paragraph 771, the Chamber found, and I quote: "That Oric was not reasonably impeded from fulfilling his duty, nor was he constrained by impossibility, and yet he preferred to do nothing." And further: "Oric wilfully decided not to do anything about it, not even at least to try and inquire about the situation of the prisoners." So the prevailing circumstances did not impede Oric's ability to perform his command function; it was his preference to do nothing. Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber's case law rules out the generally harsh or chaotic context of war as a mitigating factor for war crimes, and I point Your Honours to Blaskic appeals judgement paragraph 711 and the Bralo appeal judgement at paragraph 413. Your Honours, the Bralo case is instructive because the Trial Chamber accepted that there was a demonstrating military and political situation in Central Bosnia between 1992 and 1993, that there was tension, animosity, enormous pressure placed on everyone, and that it was notorious that such pressure existed. So the Bralo Appeals Chamber, in rejecting these factors ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry for this interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll conclude. The Trial Chamber's analysis of the prevailing situation in Srebrenica boils down to the fact that Oric was party of a very difficult war against militarily superior Serb forces in the humanitarian crisis of Srebrenica. Out of sympathy for the plight of the Bosnian Muslims, the Chamber lost sight of the gravity of the crimes at issue which should have been the pivotal sentencing consideration. Your Honours, this is a dangerous path for international criminal law to pass down. It resurrects shades of the long discredited just cause theory, whereby breaches of IHL are excused if committed by a party to the conflict with a just cause. IHL applies equally to both sides of the conflict regardless of who is militarily superior and regardless of the validity of their cause. The Chamber was wrong to treat the plight of the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica as a factor mitigating Oric's crimes, or alternatively it was wrong to give it so much weight in mitigation. Your Honours, those -- that concludes my submissions and I'll take any questions or hand the floor to Ms. Baig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There's apparently no question; however, I have to state that there are only five remaining minutes, taking into account the short break, for the Prosecution right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the very little time that remains for the Prosecution appeal, I'd like to begin by answering two of the questions raised in our addendum to the Scheduling Order. First, with regard to question 5, the Prosecution agrees with the Defence that the date of death of Mizret Halilovic was 16 January 1993, and we draw your attention to Exhibit P507E and Oric's own account in P329, tape 11, page 4. In response to question 6, the Prosecution did not argue at trial for a departure from the Appeals Chamber's Hadzihasanovic interlocutory decision of 16th July 2003. The reason for this is simple, neither the Prosecution nor the Defence at trial knew that the Trial Chamber would break-up Oric's effective control into two separate periods, before and after the 27th of November, 1992. The Defence suffered no prejudice since it fully defended against the allegations of failure to prevent and punish throughout the entire period of the crimes charged. For this same reason, the Prosecution was never in a position to argue against the Hadzihasanovic appeals decision because the factual situation arose only at the time the judgement was rendered. Given the limited time, I would refer Your Honours to our appeals brief with regard to the cogent reasons that we have advanced on appeal that directly undermine the majority of the Appeals Chamber's position that a number of instruments in international law militate against an interpretation of the customary international law norm of command responsibility which could include a successor/commander factual situation. I think that it's best that I open myself to questions if I can assist the Chamber in any way in relation to the successor/commander problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It seems not to be the case, and I think it's clearly litigated and we know about the question before us. Therefore, thank you for your submissions. The reason why we had this short break, and without any courtesy interrupting Ms. Jarvis, we thought that it would be wise to have the long lunch break already now, so that we can fully contritely listen to further submissions. I can see no objections from the parties; and, therefore, we will resume at 2.00 sharp. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand that I want to avoid the impression that we have an accused today present here, so let's change the seats first. As regards in our following schedule, as you all know, we have to change the tapes, so we can't continue until the very end of the day without having another break. We will now continue with the response and the reply, having then another break of 20 minutes and then continue as scheduled. Mr. Jones, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm obliged. I'm going to deal with the Prosecution's appeal, but not in the strict order in which they've presented it. I beg your indulgence in that respect. I deal first with the Prosecution's plea for a longer sentence, and I start with three basic principles of sentencing: Firstly, that the penalty must reflect the culpability of the offender; second, and here there's authority too abundant to mention, but that the Trial Chamber has a wide discretion in the sentence it imposes; and, thirdly, and particular to this appeal, the Appeals Chamber has held that double exposure to sentencing with the consequent stress and anxiety amounts to double jeopardy, and that's Aleksovski appeals judgement paragraphs 190 to 363. In this case, the Trial Chamber was at pains to stress the extraordinary limited basis on which they found Oric liable, and I quote: "The present case is unique in its particulars, and no real comparison can be drawn with other previous cases, both in regard to the accused's very limited responsibility and the extraordinary circumstances in which he operated." That's paragraph 780. At paragraph 771, the Chamber said: "The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that it was a short time following the replacement of Mirzet Halilovic with Atif Krdzic and the commencement of the Serb winter offensive." I break there because this was a very important part of the case, that there was this terrible offensive which would have led to the fall of Srebrenica in April 1993. We said and witnesses backed us up that what happened in July 1995, the genocide, the massacres in two or three days of 8.000 boys and men in killing fields around Srebrenica, that that would have happened in April 1993 if it hadn't been made a safe area, and that's what this winter offensive is about. So I continue: "During that time, the accused had a duty to prevent the reoccurrence of murder and cruel treatment of prisoners. During this short time, he was not reasonably impeded from fulfilling this duty, nor was he constrained by impossibility." I break there to say that is one of our ground of appeal, this impossibility test. They continue: "Yet he preferred to do nothing."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you won't come across, in our submission, words like that in any other case before this Tribunal; and the situation in 1992 to 1993, as the Chamber heard with copious evidence, was truly appalling and had the most tragic outcome of which our client was himself the victim, having lost scores of friends and relatives in the massacres in 1995. So the Trial Chamber had the benefit of hearing for a year and a half all the poignant evidence about the situation in Srebrenica, seeing the footage, amputations in the hospital without anaesthetic, and matters like that which everyone had to endure. They knew in the midst of that he displayed humanity to all, to Serb and Muslim alike. It's not evidence that we rely on; but if you look at the Prosecution's evidence of alleged visits by Oric, it's always about inquiring as to the condition of the detainees, whether they're being fed and whether they're being mistreated. We see with Halilovic his intervention there. Let's not be hypocritical, in a situation where in Srebrenica, every day people were dying from starvation from the sniping and shelling campaign by the Serbs, dying horrifically, being injured horrifically, we had a witness here who was a boy, who was blinded from a shell from the Serbs, that hearing of one detainee who had been killed or possibility, we'll come to actually what Oric heard, nonetheless, was so concerned, even though he was defending the lines against -- so they wouldn't fall to the Serbs, that he made sure the War Presidency looked into it and the person was removed. In our submission, that's a very high level of compassion and concern showed for the enemy in the midst of the most terrible adversity. So the Chamber found him liable on the narrowest possible basis, and we say they were wrong to find him liable at all. You know all of our reasons for saying that. But if you accept the conviction, if you allow the conviction to stand despite our complaints, if you are of the view that they didn't amount to errors of fact or law, and still despite all the matters we mentioned, you allow the conviction to stand, but the sentence is then viewed in isolation, and you say, simply, well, two years for war crimes, it's not enough, then that's the ultimate injustice, because the sentence is hard-wired into the whole approach taken by the Chamber to this case, into the factual matrix. You can't just extract it and look at the sentence apart from all that. We have one illustration of that which is the phrase in the judgement that, due to the ultimate disposition of this case, the Chamber was satisfied that we weren't too prejudiced by the breaches of disclosure. The Trial Chamber found the breaches of Rule 68, and it said all in all we weren't prejudiced. So what it really meant, the Trial Chamber, was that with a two-year sentence, Oric was immediately released. So the sentence reflects all sorts of thing that happened at trial; and, as I say, it can't be viewed in isolation. This finding by the Chamber of these extraordinary circumstances came from a Chamber which heard Prosecution witnesses, I'll just give you two examples, saying things such as the following: This is Nedret Mujkanovic on the 21st of February 2005, T5363, this is a doctor in the War Hospital doing heroic work savings lives there. "He was a very young person, this Oric. He carried a tremendous burden. He was only 25 years old and had no prior military experience because he used to be a policeman before that. People used to sing songs about him, so he was immortalized in several songs that were played and performed. He was known as a very brave, very able fighter. This is what people said about him in Srebrenica; this is how people saw him." Before that, he said how Oric never blew his own trumpet, if you like, but only extolled the virtues of others. Colonel Tucker, the British colonel who was awarded the military cross, with great experience in military matters, answered the following question this way. "Q. As a military commander with his appalling possibility of the lines falling, the town falling, and ensuing massacre, do you agree, as a decorated military man, that this is a terrible burden for a commander, certainly a young commander, to bear." He replied, as a Prosecution witness, Colonel Tucker, T6139: "He was operating in the most adverse and most difficult of circumstances. I cannot imagine having to operate in such circumstances." Now, the Prosecution refer to Bralo, and, in fact, they had a separate filing on Bralo, saying it is wrong for the Chamber to take into account the armed conflict because that's the very matrix in which the crimes occur. But Srebrenica, in 1992 and 1993, firstly was a million miles away from the situation in Central Bosnia; but, secondly, and this is the absolutely key point, it wasn't because the Trial Chamber because it sympathized with what he had been through, that they were giving him a lesser sentence. It was because of this appalling threat that he didn't take action, that he didn't do more to prevent crimes. That was the Trial Chamber's understanding that the reason why he didn't actually do more, and they blamed him for it. They convicted him for it. It was because he had to deal with this. So it's not that he chose sitting in tranquility and was given the option, "Well, do you want to prevent murders," and he said, "Well, no, I don't care about Serb life." It was because he was on the lines fighting to prevent thousands from being killed, and that was the crux of the Trial Chambers mitigation, if you like. I believe that's all I want to say about sentence. Turning to the ground that Oric is guilty of the murder and cruel treatment crimes that he failed to prevent, the Prosecution referred to the fact that causation isn't a requirement, as if it were relevant to this issue. Really, in our submission, causation is a red herring because, of course, the duty to punish a crime can't have a causal element because the crime already occurred. Really, all we say in relation to this ground is that there is an abundant authority for the proposition -- position taken by our Trial Chamber that the crime is a dereliction of duty offence. In ICTY law, ICTR law, Special Court for Sierra Leone recently affirmed it in the Brima and the Fofana cases. And post-World War II case law, Yamashita and High Command case, both in our submission indicate that it's a failure to discharge his duty crime. So we say no error of law has been demonstrated. The sort of policy matter, in our submission, it's not a principle to stand to say that Oric should have been found guilty of murder and cruel treatment; rather, it's a call for him to be branded with the mark of Cane, when in fact his liability is so much more attenuated. At best, it's a liability for failing to prevent subordinates from aiding and abetting by omission and it goes on; and yet the Prosecution wants the world to see Oric and say murderer. That's wrong in our submission. They also, to be fair to the Prosecution, they talk about deterrence; but to suppose that a commander in the field is going to modify his behaviour depending on whether he stands to be convicted of murder or dereliction of duty is, to our mind, completely unrealistic. That's not the sort of calculation is commander is going to enter into. Since time is short, I'll just list our authorities supporting obviously the Trial Chamber position, which say is sustainable. At Krnojelac appeals judgement, paragraph 75: "It cannot be overemphasized that where superior responsibility is concerned an accused is not charged with the crimes of his subordinates with his failure to carry out his duty as a superior to exercise control." The Bagilishema appeals judgement, paragraph 35. His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen's dissenting opinion in the Hadzihasanovic decision: "Command responsibility imposes criminal responsibility on a commander for failure to take corrective action --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- in respect to a crime committed by another; it does not make the commander a party to the crime committed by the other." Well, if it does make him a party, then, in our submission, it's not accessorial liability either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll repeat it. It was: "Command responsibility imposes criminal responsibility on a commander for failure to take corrective action in respect to a crime committed by another; it does not make the commander a party to the crime committed by that other." Judge Hunt took the same position in his dissenting opinion; the Halilovic trial judgement at paragraph 78, and the reference is there in paragraphs 38, 41, 54. Hadzihasanovic trial judgement, paragraph 75; Strugar trial judgement paragraphs 357, 359; and as I say Fofana and Brima, the CDF and RUF trials at the Special Court. We do also say that the High Command case in Yamashita has language to the same effect; but in the interest of moving on, I won't cite that. I'll just mention, in relation to the ICC, on its position of Professor Kai Ambos, that Article 28 there creates a separate dereliction of duty offence. Article 28 can be characterized as "a separate crime of omission, since it makes the superior liable only for a failure of proper supervision and control of his or her subordinates, but not," at least not directly, "for crimes that they commit." That's in the Cassese and others commentary to the ICC Statute. Just while I mention Ambos, I just want to mention Ambos, and I just want to correct one matter, which is in our response brief. We cited an article by Ambos. We had received an earlier draft where he had certain wording. Apparently, that wasn't the final draft. So, in the final article, those words don't appear, so we would withdraw those words, and apologise if anyone's been misled. So, in our submission, the case law and commentaries clearly establishes the position taken by the Trial Chamber. Now, I'd like to move on to documents as a general topic. My learned friend Mr. Rogeres referred to a number of documents in relation to their ground 1. Now, interestingly, I would like to start with what the Prosecution say in their response brief at paragraph 109, and they refer to Kunarac appeals judgement at paragraph 207, for the primacy of eye-witness testimony, and they say: "The Trial Chamber was correct to place more weight on eye-witness testimony than the documentary evidence." And that's our starting point, really. What you wouldn't understand, what you wouldn't gather from the Prosecution's presentation is how thoroughly and completely impeached their exhibits were at trial. They were impeached by witnesses or not shown to witnesses; although, there's an interpretation or a spin on the document which no witness confirmed, and that's separately one of our grounds of appeal. But just to give you a few examples. P80 was referred to by my learned friend. Now, P08, a Prosecution witness, Hakija Meholjic, said, and this is T6963: "I believe that this has nothing whatsoever to do with the reality of the situation on the ground. This looks like a very good homework somebody was given to do and did really very well." You can here the sarcasm in his voice. "However, this document has nothing whatsoever to do with the reality of the situation at the time," and other witnesses described P80 as pure fantasy, not even 100 per cent correct, et cetera. Now, can you think of a more damning enunciation of a document by a Prosecution witness and to say it has absolutely nothing to do with reality. Yet it is still relied upon by the Prosecution, and the Trial Chamber relied on it and referred to it. P109 was also referred to. That was -- the evidence is simply that was an report by the staff on formations and appointments made by the War Presidency. That was the evidence of Sacirovic at T13289. And Bogilovic, Prosecution witness, testified that the very reference in P109 to a decision of the TO staff was probably a mistaken formulation. That's T6425. No witness confirmed the truth of the contents of this document. P109 -- sorry, P4 was very similar. No witness confirmed the truth, accuracy, reliability, authenticity of P4. Many Prosecution witnesses, in fact, cast doubt on it. We've got all the references, and we provided the references. In fact, we had many of these references in an annex B to our response brief, but that was struck out. But I think you'll find in our appeals brief and our closing brief that you'll find what we say about these exhibits. And, finally, just on that, we saw this list of military police. It was said, well, it was a big unit and look at how many people were in it. But, again, one has to look at what witnesses said about this. Two witnesses said that Sead Ademovic, who appears on P590 and P609, said that he wasn't in the military police at all, and there was evidence that people on that list weren't even in Srebrenica at the time. So that paper, that exhibit is practically worthless. It's a suggestion that people were in military police which were actually not just not confirmed but impeached, and it's T13202, T14662 to 14663. What we complain of - I'm responding to the Prosecution's appeal, but I can't help also mentioning our position - is that the Trial Chamber erred terribly by regarding these as authentic, as having been proved as authentic beyond a reasonable doubt, and even beyond that committing the fallacy of thinking what if something's authenticity and its contents are true. Of course, that doesn't follow. A document can be authentic in the sense that it's properly signed by the purported author, and yet its contents are completely false. The Trial Chamber has systematically conflated those two issues. Interestingly, in looking on case law on this, I found a decision in the Blaskic Trial Chamber from the 30th of January 1998, holding that documents shown to a witness that are not identified are excluded. That happened many times in our case where the documents weren't excluded. What's interesting to know of that case is that it concerned Defence exhibits, and it's sad if there's a perception, justifiable perception, that Defence exhibits get excluded if they're not confirmed, and their not Prosecution exhibits. But why, you might wonder, why these exhibits are so unreliable, and there are two reasons which we submitted throughout the trial. The first, as the Trial Chamber found, the situation in Srebrenica was uniquely chaotic and disorganized, and, therefore, aspirations on paper often didn't reflect the reality. Prosecution witness General Delic put it and he said: "The paper will suffer anything." And when I asked him what that meant he said: "This is an expression that we use in Bosnia which means you can put anything on paper; however, when it comes to implementation, this is where the problems arise." That's T8694. Another witness said to the Prosecution: "I can't think where you get your documents from; you must have realized they contradict one another." T11153. The other reason why the documents are so unreliable is, as we pointed out, when Srebrenica fell, and with these terrible massacres, all of the documents in Srebrenica fell into the hands of the Serbs, the very forces who had the ultimate incentive to try and shift the blame if at all possible. It's been a long-term propaganda exercise on the part of the Serbs, to say that they were provoked to commit the massacres in 1995; and, of course, our client is part of that whole conspiracy theory -- well, conspiracy theory, that pretext. That's referred to at footnote 68 of the judgement.
